I noticed that the needle pointed over 30 degrees to the right as I engaged NAV - figuring something was wrong I disengaged NAV and turned back to something close to direct BLD and asked if I could just go direct BLD which I was given. narrative_1: Unanticipated GPWS warning on approach requiring crew action. We were flying the freighter (tail); second leg ZZZ-ZZZ1 (1.5 hr delayed at start of day); 5-6 hours into the flight duty period (~XA:00 pm local time). Night IMC w/moderate to heavy rain showers in vicinity. I was Pilot Flying PF (Captain).Clearance was ZZZ...ZZZ1. On the ground at ZZZ we planned and briefed the departure and RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from the ZZZZZ1 transition. De-iced; taxied; departed; climbed to cruise at FL280.Enroute to ZZZZZ1 at cruise; Center warned of areas of moderate to extreme precipitation from ZZZZZ1 fix to the airport and advised of better weather to the Northeast. After discussing a change to the arrival; we both agreed to request radar vectors to the approach segment from ZZZZZ (IAF). Center agreed to vector us around and down to put us on the published portion of the arrival with the stated intention of joining us to the approach path at ZZZZZ2. FO (First Officer) made the changes in the FMS and we briefed and then ran the Decent Checklist Change Triangles.Radar vectors included a descent and vectors resulting in established on published segment near ZZZZZ2 at 5000 and given approach clearance from center (I had directed PM to reset FMS Cruise Alt to 8;000 feet when we were on vectors). Once established near ZZZZZ2 at 5;000 cleared us for the approach. I engaged LNAV/VNAV and set airport elevation; but was high on the vertical path. I continued to slow to final configuration (gear down; Flaps 40) by ZZZZZ1; stable; but still 1;400 feet above the path in VNAV SPD (vertical navigation speed). After the turn at ZZZZZ1 I set 1;600 feet in the MCP ALT window (FAP 1;600 MSL) and at approximately 2;300 MSL; engaged Vertical Speed down in order to regain the VNAV Path before the FAP. As I approached the path; I reset MCP altitude to airfield elevation and engaged VNAV while pitch mode was in ALT ACQ (altitude acquire); resulting in an unrecognized mode change to V/S (2;100 ft/min) and projected vertical path well before the airport. It was at this point; we received a GPWS 'Caution Terrain' followed shortly by GPWS Warning 'Terrain Fly UP.'  I immediately executed an escape maneuver/go-around; climbing and flying the go-around flight path to ZZZ2 and mistakenly climbed to 5;000 MSL (missed approach alt 3;000 MSL); entering the hold as published. I requested and was given a descent to 3;000 MSL in holding.We then built and briefed the RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from ZZZ2; ran the Descent Change Triangles; received our approach clearance; and executed the approach to landing uneventfully. The FO and I thoroughly debriefed the events of the flight. I then called the Duty Pilot and DISPATCH to report the incident. I should have requested radar vectors ZZZZZ1 for the best opportunity to acquire the VNAV path. I allowed the Controller to compress and to keep me high on my approach; and reducing my situational awareness. I configured very early; but it still wasn't enough to regain the VNAV path. In the future; I will not allow the ATC Controller to dictate the terms of my energy management and will give myself the Flight Handbook recommended 3 miles per 1;000 descent planning as a minimum starting point.Because we compressed our arrival and ended up high above the VNAV path I attempted to use the Vertical Speed method on LNAV/VNAV Approach rules to regain VNAV path prior to the FAP. Had I cross-checked my FMA after selecting VNAV; I would have noticed the V/S mode and perhaps executed an uneventful go-around. In the future; I will make sure to always verify my FMA mode on the PFD after making a selection on the MCP.Lastly; after fully configuring and still not descending to the path; I might have been able to acquire VNAV path prior to the FAP using Speed Intervention. There was chance we were light enough (low Ref Speed) to accelerate the idle pitch descent to regain the path; ensuring the pitch FMA remained in VNAV and avoiding the unrecognized and inadvertent V/S mode descent that caused the GPWS Warning. Recommend expanding the understanding of VNAV speed during initial and continuing qualification training in the B737.
narrative_2: Escape Maneuver occurred at approximately (time) local time on (date). Flight conditions at the time were night; IMC; rain; light turbulence.Leg 2 of a planned 4 leg day. Leg 1 was delayed 1 hours due to cargo loading. The flight was uneventful. Deiced in ZZZ after aircraft pushback. Filed route was ZZZ...ZZZ1. We planned and briefed the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZZZ. Cruise was at FL280. PF (pilot flying) MFD was in WX Radar mode due to significant weather in the area. PM (pilot monitoring) was in TERR (terrain) mode with VSD (vertical speed) displayed. Cruise was at dusk. Shortly after starting the descent; ATC notified us that he saw an area of Moderate to Extreme precipitation ahead of us. ATC said it looked clearer to the north and asked if we would like vectors to the north for an approach via ZZZZZ1. We responded yes and he started vectoring us north. PF flew while PM loaded the arrival from ZZZZZ1 (via IAF ZZZZZ1). PM briefed the new approach and called for change triangles; which we accomplished. ATC had us do intermediate level-offs at 8;000 feet; then 7;000 feet. PF asked PM to reset the cruise altitude to provide an accurate flight path. In anticipation of being high on flight path; PF configured early to flaps 40. PM was actively monitoring the VSD and flight path; and requested lower when able from ATC. ATC said he would give us lower in a few miles. He then gave us a short vector prior to ZZZZZ2 with a descent to 6;500 feet. At approx 0.5 miles before ZZZZZ2 at 6;500 feet; ATC cleared us 'to cross ZZZZZ2 at or above 5;000 feet; cleared RNAV Rwy XX at ZZZ1'. When cleared for the approach over ZZZZZ2; PF dialed in field elevation in the MCP and descended towards the flight path. Flight conditions were night; IMC; rain; light turbulence. Approximately 1 mile prior to ZZZZZ3; we were still high on flight path so PF verbalized and set Vertical Speed down and reset MCP to 1;600 feet. PM saw the downward vector on the VSD and monitored it for approaching the flight path. Almost immediately thereafter; we received a 'Caution; Terrain' and the depicted island terrain went yellow on PM's MFD. This was quickly followed by a 'Terrain; Pull up' and the depicted terrain on the MFD went red. PF called for go-around and executed the escape maneuver. After aircraft was climbing; PF asked PM to reset MCP for missed approach altitude of 3;000 feet. PF initially had difficulty verifying the missed approach altitude on the EFB due to turbulence; transition to nighttime; and prioritizing monitoring the aircraft state while performing aircraft cleanup. PF put and verbalized 5;000 feet in the MCP window; thinking 5;000 feet was better in case 3;000 feet was incorrect. PMs intent was to devote more brain cells to performing the aircraft cleanup items and monitoring the safe aircraft state as we climbed. Aircraft was cleaned up; leveled at 5;000 feet and continued to holding at ZZZ2. We then queried ATC for a descent to 3;000 feet; setup the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZ2. Approach was briefed by Captain; flown; and landed uneventfully. Once the aircraft reached parking and shutdown at ZZZ1; Captain and FO debriefed the events. Captain called and briefed Duty Officer; who approved continuing to the remaining 2 destinations. Captain also called and spoke with Dispatch. The remaining flights to were flown with minimal changes. Post flight; the Captain called Quality Assurance to see what they could tell us; so that we could learn further from this experience.Stay on the magenta line; and if vectored off; get back on it as early as possible. Even though the controller had plans to vector us back onto the RNP approach; a better outcome likely would have resulted if we started at the IAP. This way we would have been able to descend on a normal flight path; with adequate time and pacing; vs. having to stay higher due to the controllers higher vectoring altitudes. Request the IAP next time.At nighttime in IMC; I need to have a faster response timecalling for the escape maneuver/go-around. I should clarify this maneuver more; particularly the triggers. I should have been the first to call for it since the Captain was the PF. Instead of trying to salvage a bad or difficult approach; make the decision to go-around earlier. Memorize the missed approach altitude prior to each approach; or ensure my EFB chart is not zoomed-in so far that I cannot see it without a quick glance.Clarify various 'what-if scenarios' on RNP approaches; Escape Maneuvers; Go-Arounds. If I haven't flown as much recently; spend extra time clarifying. Communicate with Center that 6;500 feet at ZZZZZ2 creates a very difficult approach to accomplish. Recommend to them that vectoring to the IAF is likely a better option.
synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported executing an escape maneuver due to a CFIT event resulting from a compressed approach clearance. Crew completed subsequent approach in an uneventful landing.

I verified if he was lined up for the correct runway and on very short final; he appeared to maneuver for the correct runway.Background: all controllers at ZZZ have been on 6 day work week for the last few months due to a shortage in staffing. Our facility has also been experiencing roughly a 20% increase in traffic volume compared to last year. In September; our traffic count index has reached the numbers for us to qualify for a level 8 upgrade. If we sustain our traffic numbers for the next couple of months; level 8 at ZZZ will become a reality once it gets approved by the National Validation Team.We are all fatigued from the increase in traffic and the amount of overtime we have all been working. Even though we have a staffing issue; due to the compressed tour hours; there is a good amount of overlap between controllers so we can keep LC split into 2 positions. narrative_2: While on a Class B clearance through the Class Bravo airspace on published VFR Route southbound at 5;500 feet; I received a traffic notification from Approach for traffic at 11 o'clock; opposite direction; at 5;000 MSL a conflict for traffic that was approaching nearly head-on. I continued to visually scan for the traffic in front of me; and when I finally spotted the oncoming traffic it was at my 11 o'clock to 11:30 position in my windscreen; at eye level. I was unable to discern any relative motion of the target relative to my windscreen. The only change I could see in the target was that it was getting larger in my field of view; and that it appeared to be some type of small jet aircraft. I immediately initiated a turn to my right in order to avoid the oncoming traffic. The turn that I initiated was done very quickly; and was probably on the order of a 30 to 35 degree angle of bank. As a result of this turn; I lost approximately 250 feet of altitude from my cruising altitude of 5;500 feet. My change in heading was approximately 45 degrees; and once my turn was completed I was able to discern relative motion of the target with respect to my windscreen and left side window. The traffic was now moving to my left; and the separation between the two of us was increasing.The opposite directly traffic passed well behind me. At that point the TRACON Controller called me and admonished me for deviating from my assigned heading and altitude. I responded to the controller with an apology; and explained that the opposite direction traffic appeared to be on a collision course with me; and it required me to take evasive action. The controller provided me with a toll-free number to call after I landed. After landing I called the toll-free number and spoke to an individual at SOCAL who asked me to describe the occurrence from my perspective. I described the occurrence in an identical manner to what I have written here. The individual was very courteous and listened carefully to my explanation; and thanked me for calling. The call ended with no indication to me that any further action would be forthcoming.It is extremely difficult to estimate lateral and vertical separation of traffic; especially when a target has no apparent relative motion and is approaching head-on. Any vertical separation that does exist between two aircraft in this situation will not be perceptible until the aircraft are very close together; when there is very little time to take evasive action if it is required. In this particular case; the opposite direction traffic was probably traveling at least twice as fast as my aircraft; resulting in an effective rate of closure of at least 400 MPH. A vertical separation of 500 feet is very small; and when possible sources of altitude error are included; it is possible that the actual vertical separation between our two aircraft was less than 500 feet.  Approximately ten minutes after this occurrence; I was in the vicinity of another airport and was in contact with another sector of the TRACON. This Controller provided me with a traffic advisory regarding jet traffic inbound from the west at 5;000 feet; and gave me instructions to climb and maintain 6;000 feet for separation purposes. I initiated the climb and leveled off at 6;000 feet; and observed the jet traffic passed well below me. After the jet traffic had crossed my flight path; the Controller cleared me back down to 5;500 feet. I have included a description of this action on the part of Approach as an example of prudent traffic management.In summary; I should have been more diligent in maintaining my assigned altitude of 5;500 feet during my turn to avoid the oncoming traffic. However; it was my belief that there was insufficient separation between the flight paths of our two aircraft; and seeing no relative motion of a target that was at eye-level in my windscreen; as pilot-in-command of the aircraft I took evasive action in the interest of collision avoidance.

narrative_1: This event was a complex setup with numerous contributing factors that led to a slight and uneventful course deviation on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. In preparing the flight; I ran a prelim flight plan which recommended a route I would expect; a SID that meshed with the ZZZZZ3 arrival to ZZZ1. It was presumed this route was preferred to accommodate the numerous TFR's. I know for certain in the app I had selected FL230 as I wanted to either be rerouted as necessary for the TFRs or be above as the TFRs were below FL180. These issues were disclosed; briefed between the two pilots prior to filing flight plan; discussed verbally in the takeoff briefing; and even added extra fuel for possible reroute. When our clearance was obtained to depart ZZZ; it was for the SID and Victor airways as filed with app; further reinforcing the presumption that it was ATC preferred due to the TFR's. Traffic was light; and Ground Control stated Runway XXC was available which we accepted. This now being a very short taxi. I reminded him that we were instructed to maintain 4;100 feet until established and that we were cleared for the ILS. The Captain was navigating in pink needles and I had green needles on my side so that the Captain could reference the glide slope. We were showing approximately a dot and a half above the glide slope. At that point the Captain began to descend to catch up to the glide slope and proceeded to turn inbound. As far as I could tell he started doing this prior to being established inbound. Once we were finally established inbound we were at approximately 3;800 feet and descending which was above the minimum altitude for that segment however we were instructed to maintain 4;100 feet until established on a segment. At this point the controller switched us over to advisories. The flight continued normally. The controller did not advise us of any issues. This was all under visual conditions. I don't believe the altitude was a problem. I think we were within the normal tolerances for being established on the inbound course however I am uncertain. This report is being filed because the Captain prematurely descended below our assigned altitude as well as both the Captain and I feeling as though the controller was very unprofessional and unhelpful in aiding us in flying the plane the safest way possible. The Captain and I realized that we couldn't find the appropriate fix for the procedure turn in the box and did the right thing by telling the controller and trying to work with him. He was not very receptive to helping. As I said this created confusion in the cockpit trying to figure out how to make the procedure turn happen. As mentioned; after asking several times we were finally cleared direct ZZZZZ1. Approaching ZZZZZ1 at 4;100 feet and seeing we were high; the Captain disconnected the autopilot and started descending. That's when I reminded him that we needed to maintain 4;100 feet until established and weren't quite at ZZZZZ1 yet. He responded by saying he had the field and that it was ok to start descending. The root cause of all of this was the controller refusing to accommodate our requests to start the ILS [Runway] XX at a fix that would eliminate an NDB procedure turn. The end result was us getting a compromise for flying the approach we needed however it left us high which lead the Captain to descend early to catch the glide slope. As mentioned we reacted by asking the controller several times to work with us. We weren't asking for much. All we wanted was to be cleared to a fix to give us space to set up and [eliminate] the procedure turn. As far as the Captain possibly starting his descent early; I reacted by speaking up and telling him that I didn't think we were established inbound yet. He elected to continue to descend despite the concerns. This was a one leg day. Day one of a four day trip. Starting your first leg at XA:00 is tough for anyone. Being tired from sitting around all day waiting to go to work; we figured the safest option was to ask for a solution that eliminated the NDB procedure turn. We were both confused in trying to set up the box and asked for a different fix; ZZZZZ1; which seemed like a good option. This was the right decision. We did not expect so much push back from the controller. The last time I did any NDB procedures was almost five years ago in a simulator. With GPS waypoints and our FMS; the safest option was to avoid trying to experiment with an NDB procedure turn while conducting a revenue flight at night. Additionally; although instructed to be at 4;100 feet at ZZZZZ1 which would leave us slightly high; it would have been a better option if the Captain had let the auto pilot turn inbound and as soon as we were established then he could have initiated the descent to catch up to the glide slope. Since I was in 5/5 VMC conditions; and there was no other observed traffic in the vicinity of the airport; I cancelled IFR approximately 10-12 miles from the airport after having it in sight. I elected to enter the pattern on an extended left base for landing on Runway XX and made the appropriate radio call on the CTAF frequency. While on base; I began to descend below 1;032 feet MSL (the approximate normal pattern altitude) to approximately 700 feet MSL and initiated a left turn to final; approximately 2 miles from the XX runway threshold. As I made the turn to final; I allowed my altitude to fall to approximately 400 feet MSL (this was directly over the waterway; so it was also approximately 400 feet AGL). I made my final approach radio call and upon realizing I was somewhat low and below the desired glidepath on final. I initiated a correction and maintained that altitude until I was able to intercept the correct glidepath and had a red and white indication on the airport Runway XX PAPI. At that point I was perhaps a little over a mile from the airport threshold. From there I proceeded to a normal final approach and landing. My flight hours shown above are approximate; I am away from home as I file this report and thus do not have access to my logbook.

I had not flown for about 5 weeks and the Captain had just done landings class at training after not flying since March; as I recall.  This was the Captain's first trip since then.After takeoff; Captain was hand flying the airplane and I was performing PM duties.  We were on the ZZZZZ2 departure and I had checked in with ZZZ Departure.  They told us about a storm directly to our south that other flights were having to leave the departure route to avoid.  ATC said we could continue to the west and turn to a 150 heading when able.  After looking at the radar return I acknowledged the instruction and added we would have to go about another 10 miles west.  ATC acknowledged and cleared us to climb to 12;000 feet.I should also mention this was in a very compressed time line.  Tower turned us over to Departure; I was doing the After Takeoff Check and making FMC modifications under the Captain's instructions; and checking in and talking with ATC.  The plane was also very light; so we were climbing rapidly.  I was interrupted three times while trying to read the After Takeoff Checklist and I think we were nearly at 10;000 feet by the time I was able to accomplish the checklist.  I guess; what I'm trying to say is; I felt that I was very busy; and surprisingly so.  ZZZZZ can get busy; apparently even now; but the thunderstorm and the communication and coordination involved with that probably took us to task saturation.After being cleared to 12;000; we got another frequency change and ATC cleared us to 14;000 feet.  I set it in the MCP and saw the flight director was still in LNAV and commanding a left turn.  I asked if Captain wanted HDG SEL and Captain did which I accomplished.  ATC then asked us about the turn to the south and I answered we still were going to have to go further west; but the tops were lowering and I thought the turn could be made soon.  ATC then amended our cleared altitude to 12;000 feet again.I reset the MCP again and got acknowledgment from the Captain.  ATC then cleared us to go direct to ZZZZZ1 when we were able.  I put it in the FMC to see how the course looked compared to the radar return.  I looked out the window to see how the tops were looking.  I heard the altitude alert chime then looked at our altimeter and saw we were climbing through 12;000 feet.  I immediately exclaimed we were cleared to 12;000 feet and I think the Captain swore and immediately reversed the climb.ATC then informed us we were cleared to 12;000 feet.  I re-acknowledged the altitude clearance and we descended back to 12;000 feet.  I don't think we got above 12;600 feet.I wish I could remember when we were re-cleared to 12;000 feet; because I don't remember hearing the approaching altitude alert chime.  I think the altitude may have been above 11;000 feet so we were already within the 900 foot alert window.  When the chime did sound; I thought it was the 900 feet to go; but it was really the 300 foot off warning.
narrative_2: We were on the departure and had been told to maintain a heading due to weather. Altitude clearance was to 14;000 feet. A series of instructions came regarding weather deviations; cleared to a fix when able; etc. Somewhere in here our altitude clearance was modified to 12;000 feet. We were discussing our strategy with regards to getting back on course when the FO realized and announced I had passed 12;000 feet and was at 12;400 feet. I still had 14;000 feet in my mind as our clearance limit. Neither of us remembers an altitude warning horn sounding as we passed 11;000 feet. We both felt task saturated at the time. Neither pilot has been actively flying over the past several months; and currency/recency of experience was absolutely a contributing factor.
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a track and altitude deviation during departure.  Flight crew cited task saturation and lack of flying were contributing factors.

narrative_1: We were departing from Pittsburgh Airport. We took off on runway 28R and were assigned runway heading.Our flight plan first fix was AHTIY (then to BURGS). We briefed the route during preflight and of course verified that the course looked like it should.Shortly after takeoff; we were given a turn to the left to 'eighty' which I know from prior experience is how they pronounce that first fix; AHTIY. We brought that point up in our flight plan; inserted it into the FMS (Flight Management System) direct; agreed; then activated. The turn was a very sharp left. Once we realized we were turning toward the airport and away from our course; we briefly discussed amongst ourselves that the seemed strange. I immediately called up to verify that our clearance was a left turn direct 'eighty' (or AHTIY.) ATC (Air Traffic Control) confirmed but immediately told us to turn right to a heading of 180 'one eighty'. We started a turn to 180 but it only added to the confusion because now I thought that perhaps when I had heard 'eighty' earlier maybe I misunderstood and it was actually a heading of 'one eighty'.Once we were on that heading; we were cleared again 'direct AHTIY'. I read it back very slowly and asked to confirm that we would make a right turn direct to the fix. He said; 'Affirmative... Direct Alpha Hotel Tango India Yankee.' It was then that I realized that the point I had on my flight plan in the FMS had the T & the I switched... AHITY. I proceeded to type in the correct spelling; we agreed and flew toward AHTIY. At this point; I thought that the point AHITY actually existed over the top of Pittsburgh Airport. I found that to be a really strange placement for such a closely spelled GPS (Global Positioning System) fix to AHTIY. Upon beginning this report; I looked at my charts to verify where that fix was located. The fix doesn't seem to exist. I racked my brain to try to figure out how the fix existed in that plane but not on my chart. Then I remembered that pilots can create their own waypoints. Normally; if a fix does not exist; the FMS pulls up an option to create a pilot waypoint. I can tell you with 100% certainty but this did not happen to me when I was entering the flight plan. However; because it took my false waypoint without the prompt to create it; I can deduce that someone created that way point in that database prior to my typing it. At this point; someone must have created a misspelled version of AHTIY as AHITY. It was then that I remembered a detail that I had deemed unimportant prior to this. When we began entering the flight plan; the First Officer was holding the paperwork. He had started to enter the flight plan and then stopped. When I asked if he was doing it or if he wanted me to; he said that he decided to stop and get the ATIS (Automatic Terminal Information Service) first so I could do it. He spelled the first point for me as AHITY and I typed it. I then picked up the other copy of the flight plan and told him I would use that for the routing if he wanted to get the ATIS. I continued with BURGS and so on. I wanted to confirm my suspicions about this waypoint so I looked up the crew for the outbound flight on that aircraft. The First Officer happens to be a friend of mine. I called her and I asked her to pull up the pilot created waypoint list. She did; and sure enough there was a fix called AHITY. I had her take a photo of the coordinates for that point and send it to me. I also asked her to please delete the point from the database. I spoke with my First Officer today about user created waypoints. He says he did not create AHITY. Either way; it was a point in the pilot waypoint database and thus allowed me to use it in my flight plan.An unfortunate series of events seems to have led up to us turning toward a non-existent point. Luckily there was no mention of pilot deviation or loss of separation with any aircraft; but a mistake was still made.In the future; I will make apoint to double check the spelling of all waypoints along the route myself. We did not catch it on our verbal route review because we read it as the first fix despite the 2 letters being switched. It didn't look much different. I have certainly learned a lot from this experience; and will do my best to ensure that this does not happen again to me or anyone that I fly with. The only suggestion I have is perhaps to request that the company send a reminder to the pilot group to refresh everyone about pilot created waypoints. I would emphasize that if you do create a waypoint; you should only do it if you are doing it purposefully and using the coordinates on your chart. Then; after the flight; you should delete that point so that we don't have non-existent points in our database.
synopsis: EMB 175 flight crew reported brief heading deviation that resulted from a non-existent waypoint entered into the Flight Management System.

narrative_1: Vectored off of ZZZZZ 4 STAR and directed to descend to 5;000 feet and proceed direct to ZZZZZ and intercept the Runway XXL LOC. Loaded ZZZZZ in FMS; selected LNAV and armed LOC. While on a roughly southwest heading and proceeding direct to ZZZZZ in LNAV/VNAV; but still well east of Runway XXL we experienced a false LOC capture and the AFDS turned the aircraft to a heading of 176 degrees. Disconnected AFDS and de-armed the LOC and then used HDG Select to turn back to ZZZZZ. While in the process of turning back to ZZZZZ; Approach Control called us and said 'Flight AAAB I need you direct to ZZZZZ; turn right heading XXX.' We proceeded direct to ZZZZZ and landed uneventfully.PF and PM both recently returned to flying after long layoffs and that may have contributed. I knew for sure not to arm the Approach (APP) mode too early due to the aircraft either climbing to join the glide slope or descending on the glide slope before being established on the localizer; and was aware of the possibility of false localizer capture; but had never experienced a false LOC capture before.Using LNAV to intercept the LOC is a normal procedure; but possibly don't arm not only the APP mode; but also the LOC until within a few degrees of the ILS final approach course.  However this procedure could cause its own set of problems/conflicts by setting you up for flying through the LOC if you forget to arm the LOC.
narrative_2: We were assigned 5;000 feet; and given direct to ZZZZZ with instructions to join the localizer for [Runway] XXL there. Captain selected ZZZZZ and we proceeded direct in LNAV mode. He also armed LOC. About 8-10 miles northeast of ZZZZZ the aircraft falsely captured the localizer and began a turn south. Captain tried to select heading mode; but it initially would not select due to the false LOC capture. When we realized what happened; he deselected the LOC mode and began our turn back to ZZZZZ. About halfway through the turn back; ATC called and said he needed us direct ZZZZZ. We informed him we were in the turn; proceeded to ZZZZZ; and completed the approach without incident.The main cause was the premature capture of the localizer. I have not seen the aircraft do this before; and don't recall a warning or admonishment that it may. I don't plan on selecting LOC until closer to the intercept fix from now on; but I still don't believe this to be a crew error except that a slightly more timely response to the errant capture probably could have happened. The delay in response may have been quicker with a bit more recency of experience as both the Captain and I had recently returned from months long absences.Delaying LOC arming until closer to intercept is what I plan to do; though I don't think that is a perfect solution. I will study my manuals to try to determine why it happened; and a closer monitoring of the system should catch the fault earlier in the errant turn.
synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported a false localizer capture; they were slow to react to the event and a track deviation occurred. The pilots stated an extended period of time off was a factor in their reaction time.

narrative_1: The Captain and I discussed not doing a Visual Approach. Passing through about 9;000 feet; we were going direct to the FAF; conditions where ceiling and visibility unlimited. Approach cleared us for a Visual Approach. We accepted and started descending to 7;000 feet; the altitude for FAF. At about 7;300 or 7;200 feet ATC advised us the Minimum Vectoring Altitude was 7;500 feet. The Captain immediately stopped descending and went to 7;500 feet until just outside the FAF. We made a normal stable approach.We didn't want to do a Visual Approach when we briefed it. We were lured in by the visual conditions and the fact that that everything was stable and non rushed. It was late. Lesson is; do not do night visuals at airports that you are not to familiar with; try to do what you brief especially around terrain. I did get distracted when I lost my flight deck WiFi when I was trying to pull up a new ATIS on iPad. Don't do visual approaches at night; especially near terrain. Fly what you brief.
narrative_2: While descending on the arrival and approximately 10 miles south of ZZZ; ATC asked us to report the field in sight. It was clear and unlimited visibility. So we called it. When cleared visual [Runway] XXL; I began a descent out of 9;000 feet. I felt that we were within the airspace; but when descending to the FAF altitude of 7;000 feet and at approximately 7;200 feet; we got a call from ATC saying altitude alert. Climb to 7;500 [feet] min vectoring altitude. We immediately climbed to 7;500 [feet] and continued approach. ATC handed us to Tower and nothing else said.During cruise; my First Officer and myself went through all company pages and arrival and approach plates. We discussed terrain and even said that we shouldn't accept a visual approach since it was night time. However; we got direct to FAF and not a usual vector outside the FAF. ATC asked us to report the field. We both evaluated that we were comfortable accepting the visual. We should have stayed with the plan because after being cleared approach; we descended below the ATC min vectoring altitude. Bottom line; be conservative and when flying approaches at night; I will no longer accept a visual approach.

narrative_1: During operation of Aircraft X at FL340 we began having GPS navigational issues. Beginning in an area approximately 40 miles SE of ALS (Alamosa VOR) along our route to approximately 80 miles SW of RSK (Rattlesnake VOR); approximately 160-200 miles; we experienced intermittent 'GPS PRIMARY LOST' messages. As we began to troubleshoot the issue we discovered that both GPS #1 and #2 were erratically receiving GPS signals; varying from 0 to 9 satellites. The system cycled rather rapidly between the GPS 1 & 2 signal strength and navigational capability; losing all GPS capability at times.  We referred to the QRH but began to surmise that given the unusual operation of the receivers that there was nothing wrong with the onboard equipment and there must be an external issue like 'jamming'. We were discussing a plan: return to land base NAV and advise ATC or request ATC temporary headings when ATC asked if we were going direct to 'DAFNY'. We advised him that we were experiencing various NAV downgrades and asked for heading verification. He gave us a heading correction of 5 degrees left. Immediately after that transmission another aircraft reported the exact same issue with GPS NAV. After a few minutes the controller advised us that there were GPS jamming exercises going on in the area around White Sands. Therefore; we updated our heading with ATC as we progressed. A subsequent controller cleared us direct to 'ZZZZZ' and advised us we appeared to be slightly north of a direct route to 'DAFNY'. Shortly thereafter 'GPS PRIMARY' returned and normal operations ensued. We continued the arrival while checking our radar position with ATC. No further anomalies were encountered. Landed without further incident in ZZZ. I can only presume that the US Government (Military) was performing 'GPS Jamming' exercises as the controller said such activities were happening around the White Sands area. How about a NOTAM!
narrative_2: At FL340 we began to get several GPS Primary Lost indications. Navigation reliability was in question so we got vectors from ATC for the fix that we were cleared to. Multiple other aircraft in the vicinity were reporting the same issues with their GPS. ATC informed us there was 'jamming' going on at nearby White Sands. When our GPS finally seemed to be working again; we were several miles off course going to the assigned fix. We reported that our GPS seemed to be working again and we were cleared to a different fix. No further anomalies were encountered but I am writing this report because were were off course for a short amount of time. White Sands jamming of GPS reported by ATC.
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported loss of GPS signal in cruise operations reportedly due to GPS jamming exercises.

narrative_1: During vectors into OKC from the east; the Approach Controller assigned us Runway 17R differently from the one we had setup (17L). After re-configuring for the ILS 17R; I asked the Pilot Monitoring to brief the approach so I can concentrate on flying (Approximately 14;000 feet MSL and descending to 4;000 feet). During the brief a bright shining white light; like a spotlight shined at us; caught our attention and cause a distraction. We still conducted the briefing; including the highest elevation figure. As I kept flying I was paying attention if the light shined us again; in the event it was a laser that needed to be reported. I had the terrain page setup from the previous briefing and both pilots were aware of the obstacle northeast of the airport (Antenna 2758 feet MSL). After the briefing was complete; we were given a vector (a 90 degree angle) for the approach within a close proximity of the Final Approach Fix (minimum altitude at FAF 3;000 feet MSL). This vector would have flown us south of the obstacle depicted in the plan view section of the approach chart. Approximately 18NM from the airport the Approach Controller queried the visual contact of the airport. Pilot Monitoring told me he had contact with it and after I picked it up in sight I asked to call for it if he still had it. At that point the Approach Controller cleared us for the visual approach for [Runway] 17R. Slightly after; the Approach Controller notified us of traffic on the approach to the parallel runway. Both pilots were trying to ID the traffic since it was below our altitude and we had to cross his approach path. We seemed clear of the traffic; but a strong wind from the south was drifting us north which cause a concern for us due to the known obstacle. The aircraft was just approaching 4;000 feet of altitude and started to level off; when I set 3;000n in the Altitude Select box. The aircraft transitioned into a shallow descent instead of holding 4;000 since it wasn't fully captured. While having a discussion about the wind I adjusted my heading and kept the descent to 3;000 feet so we could be close to level and slow when we intercepted the course outside of the FAF. Around 3500 feet we both remembered the obstacles when we saw its lights ahead and below us. I already started a transition into a climb when the Pilot Monitoring verbally reminded me of the obstacles. During the climb we got a 'Caution Obstacle'; due to the projected descent; which was removed shortly since we were already compensating. We were 500 to 700 feet above the highest obstacle. The obstacle represented on the MFD was not the highest elevation figure on the IAP chart. This depicted obstacle was part of another group of towers not depicted on the chart but they can be seen on the VFR chart in the Jeppesen app. Since it was a visual approach; I had focused on maintaining the airport inside; and started to descend and slow down so we could be on a good position for the stable approach. Following the event; we landed with no issues and had a discussion at the gate on how we could have mitigated our error. We were below the MSA and had loss awareness of the obstacles due to other distractions and the tight vector to the approach with the visual approach. Several factors played key roles for the loss of situational awareness that led us to be at a lower altitude for our location. Flags:-A night Visual approach into an airport were an obstacle is a threat.-A night Visual approach to an airport were the elevation of the airport is higher than we are normally used to.-An arrival consisting of an extended base into a visual approach rather than a downwind arrival.-The change of runway that led to a new setup and briefing.-The distractions caused by the wind-drift; traffic; and the bright light.-The tight vector given and accepted for the original approach. Our error was the premature descent to 3000 feet with the goal of not being high once we intercept the final course with short distance to the final fix. Although the setup for the approach included the awareness of terrain and using the terrain displayed as an aid; we should have use TEM to establish a plan to avoid the premature descent. A briefed plan of using the last assigned altitude of 4;000 feet until intercepting would have avoided this. During the approach brief; I should have asked my Pilot Monitoring to intervene in the event I set a lower altitude while maneuvering for the visual (mitigation plan in the vent of losing SA). I realized that our briefings cover informational items that could be threats but we should discuss mitigating plans for them. Other actions that could have been taken are: 1) denying the visual at night due to the obstacle; 2) requesting a vector for the visual; and 3) querying if a lower altitude was needed which would have led the Controller to keep us at 4;000 feet.
narrative_2: I was Pilot Monitoring. Approximately 20min out we were giving the option to change our landings intentions from [Runway] 17L to 17R which we took. Captain asked me if I could brief the approach which I did and then we performed the runway change items from the checklist. During this briefing moment we both noticed a bright light from about a 12 o'clock position which caught our attention. Captain was aware of the obstacles to the northeast of the airport (antennas) and turned on the terrain. At approximately 18 miles out we were asked if we had the airport in sight. We both saw it and were cleared for the visual approach Runway 17R. Winds were out of the south at approximately 26kt pushing us to the north since we were coming from the east. We were at 4;000 ft. and began a gradual descent. ATC advised us of traffic at 11 o'clock landing on the parallel runway. Looking for the traffic we began to noticed the red lights of the obstacles (towers) on the northeast of the airport. I pointed them out as [did] the Captain. The altitude window was set for 3;000 ft. we were currently at 3;400 ft. Captain turned off the autopilot and began a climb. As we were climbing we received a Caution for the obstacle but it cleared quickly since the Captain had already began the climb. Once cleared we continue to intercept the final approach course and perform a normal landing. We both had a long discussion after the flight and both agreed that we should had mitigated this by simply staying at 4;000ft when cleared for the visual approach since we knew about the MSA which is 3;800 ft. Also the parallel traffic played a role on this since we started looking for it due to it being in our path for intercepting the final approach course of [Runway] 17R. As a Pilot Monitoring I should had advised the Captain that selecting 3;000 ft. and continuing the descent once cleared for the visual would had put us close to the highest obstacle stated in the approach plate. I will keep this in consideration for future flights to come ensuring we are not at a lower altitude than the MSA not established on a final approach course as well as keeping in mind obstacles around us at all times.

narrative_1: Aircraft X was on heading 360 and instructed to descend to 6;000 ft.  I observed Aircraft X descend through 6;000 and at 5;800 I issued a low altitude alert; the MVA was 5;600.  Aircraft X did not respond and kept descending.  I issued another low altitude alert; climb and maintain 6;000 immediately and when their data block displayed 5;100 they reported level at 6;000.  I told them altitude indicates 5;100; they asked to verify altimeter 30.25 and I gave them the current altimeter 29.24.  After a couple miles they showed a climb and climbed to 6;000.It was apparent watching the replay that Aircraft X check on indicating 12;100 and reporting level at 13;000.  For some reason I did not catch it.  I even descended them to 8;000 and they leveled at an indicated 7;000 and I did not notice.  I think this is because 7;000 is a normal altitude that I would descend them to at that location but I had left them a little higher.  When I descended them to 6;000 and they indicated lower it was apparent something was wrong and I was immediately concerned about the MVA so I issued a low altitude alert before they went below the MVA and a climb to 6;000.A snowstorm had just blown through the airspace and there was still stiff winds out of the west gusting to 30 kts.  I had a sequence developing for ZZZ and Aircraft X was near the front of it.  I recall planning ahead; looking at strips; using the STARS (Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System) to determine how much the wind was pushing the vectors.  Also ZZZ had many taxiways closed from the snow so I was vectoring for much greater distance than usual (10 miles on final).  I must not have looked at Aircraft X's altitude when they checked on and just used the reported altitude.  While I am happy I got a low altitude alert out when they were near terrain; I wish that I had caught it on check-on.I found it strange that their altitude in STARS was accurate but not in the cockpit.  I thought the altimeter setting would change what STARS reported. I have to be diligent to verify altitudes when the aircraft check on; so altimeter discrepancies can be caught early.
narrative_2: Descending into ZZZ through FL 180 we completed the Approach Checklist and verified 30.24 altimeter setting. On vectors to final as we were leveling off; Approach Control asked us to climb to 6;000 ft. We were indicating 6;300 at that time; so the clearance just sounded odd. The Approach Controller said that we were at 5;200 and for us to climb to 6;000 and turn to a heading of 030. I immediately clicked the autopilot/auto-throttles off and started my turn towards 030 heading and started climbing; as my Pilot Monitoring verbalized that we had the wrong altimeter setting of 30.24 instead of 29.24. We leveled off at 6;000 on a 030 heading; and at that time I engaged the autopilot and auto-throttles. We got vectored for approach and landed uneventfully on Runway XX. We were asked to contact TRACON on landline by the Ground Controller as we taxied to the gate. We realized that we had unintentionally set altimeter setting of 30.24 in error instead of 29.24 which directly led to the altitude deviation. We failed to catch our error during crosschecks as we ran the checklist due to expectation bias. Lack of digital ATIS was also a contributing factor; however; we should have trapped this error as we updated the new weather. We needed to be more vigilant to trap these kind of errors.

narrative_1: We briefed the route and departure; to include the [engine failure] procedures. We confirmed the route in the FMS. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; We turned to heading 189 and hit moderate or greater turbulence and mountain waves; which significantly affected us. I had trouble communicating with ATC and performing cockpit duties due to turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 AGL; Tower said switch to departure. Upon contacting departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to a fix'; but the radio quality of the transmission was poor and we couldn't clearly hear the name of the fix. I realized the mountain was on our path and for an immediate left turn to avoid terrain. The Spokane Departure Controller cleared us direct to a fix by name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling; which I couldn't understand due to significant turbulence and poor radio quality. We continued normal flap retraction callouts and takeoff profile. We were given heading a 120; to which we turned; and it took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. We were mistakenly trying to navigate to ENY VOR which caused us to be confused and task saturated. Once we got the correct identifier for HIA and entered into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. This caused the controller to get a low altitude alert although we did not receive any terrain avoidance warnings from our aircraft. In retrospect; the controller admitted on our phone conversation afterwards that this situation is very common. There are a lot of risks and stressors associated with this MZULA.MSO RWY12 and I feel like our outside resources did not help the flight crew. We accept full responsibility for allowing this situation to develop; but changes to this procedure will greatly increase safety in the future.First our Jeppesen charts had no verbal narrative and left us needing FAA charts to understand the procedure. It would be a great help if the procedure could be simplified or the controller's expectations that are outside the procedure could be communicated before we hit significant turbulence. The controller was clearly frustrated with us which only made our situation worse by trying to give us a phone number during a high stress and high workload phase of flight in significant turbulence. This shows the controllers are not fully aware of what human factors the flight crews have and how to help safety of flight. Having poor radio transmission quality was also a significant factor.
narrative_2: I was the First Officer and Pilot Flying departing MSO. I received and read back the clearance from ATC which included the MZULA5 Departure MSO transition. I programmed this into our FMS and the Captain and I thoroughly reviewed the route in the FMS and on our Jeppesen plates. We also briefed the procedure for engine failure departure. In my takeoff briefing I again described the departure we were assigned. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; I turned to heading 189 as charted. Immediately we began to encounter moderate turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 ft AGL; Tower said switch to Departure. Upon contacting Departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to ________ ' but it was very turbulent and we did not clearly hear the name of the fix. I immediately realized the flight director was not commanding a left turn in accordance with the charted procedure. The Captain asked to say again the fix; and the controller said the name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling. At 1;000 ft AGL; I called out 'flight level change'; followed by the normal flap retraction callouts and told him we needed a left turn since I knew from the charted SID that's what we were supposed to do. Meanwhile the Captain was trying to get clarification on the fix to which we were to proceed. We knew it would be a left turn so he asked for a left turn and we were given heading 120; to which we turned. During this entire time it was very turbulent and took a lot of effort and concentration to focus on safe flying. It took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. Once we got the correct identifier and entered it into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However; this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. During this time; we had terrain radar displayed on our MFD and were well aware of our surroundings and the location of rising terrain; and at no time did we ever get a terrain caution or warning.Although the SID was correctly programmed into the FMS; for unknown reasons the Flight Director did not command the left turn to intercept the MSO 159 radial. The extreme turbulence and difficulty understanding ATC instructions caused a delay in turning to the assigned fix; resulting in a course deviation. First of all; given our route of flight; it would have made much more sense if; in the pre-departure clearance; we would have been given the Salmon transition. This fact was even stated by the ATC supervisor on the phone when I called him after we landed. He further stated they have had frequent problems with pilots and aircraft not following the procedure we were assigned. Second; I could have anticipated a potential issue; and tuned the MSO VOR in NAV 1 and 2; along with the radial to intercept prior to takeoff. If I return to MSO in the future; I will definitely do that as a backup in case this kind of thing should happen again. I realized we were supposed to be turning left; which is why we asked for a left turn in the interim while trying to get the identifier for the fix and get that loaded in the FMS. The significant turbulence and the communication difficulties with ATC were definitely contributing factors in this temporary deviation. Nonetheless; as a pilot it is my responsibility to safely and correctly fly the plane; so I will ensure I have a backup navigation source programmed and ready in the future. And if I go back there again and get assigned that same SID; I will ask for the Salmon transition rather than the MSO transition; as suggested by the ATC supervisor. Finally I will brief my Captain on what happened previously so we can be vigilant and prepared.
synopsis: Flight crew reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC departing MSO when they had a track deviation following communication difficulties.

narrative_1: We had just switched on to approach frequency and were given a heading and altitude for the visual approach. We both heard the altitude clearance as 5;000 ft. and the PM read back 5;000 ft. A few min after we had leveled off at 5;000 ft. ATC asked us to confirm altitude and gave us the altimeter. We responded with 5;000 ft. and verified we had the correct altimeter. ATC then responded the minimum vectoring altitude was 5;300 ft. for that area. As the PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to clarify we read back 5000 ft. in the initial clearance; I started a climb to 5;300 ft. ATC then asked if we had the field in sight which we did and then we were cleared for the visual approach using the GPS 14 approach plate as guidance. We landed normally.The cause of this event was a miscommunication with ATC. We both heard 5;000 ft. in the initial clearance not 5;300 ft. The PM read back 5;000 ft. and we didn't hear a correction from ATC. A contributing factor in my opinion was the fact that we were experiencing light to occasional moderate turbulence for most of the flight including the descent and that could have caused us to miss hear the original clearance and potentially the read back was hard for ATC to hear due to the PM's mic being jostled.In cases such as this we could have requested clarification if the altitude didn't sound correct but in my estimation the clearance seemed to make sense based on our position and the airport elevation and the location of obstacles and terrain which were not a factor from the direction we were arriving and they also seemed to be similar to the altitudes we would expect if on the GPS approach we were using as a backup. But it would be prudent in the future especially in turbulence to verify clearances considering the effect turbulence could have on radio transmissions.
narrative_2: We had just checked in with approach and they gave use a heading to turn to for vectors and an altitude to descend to. I thought I had remembered reading backing 5;000 ft. as the captain who was the PF put 5;000 ft. in the FMA and we both confirmed the 5;000 ft. once set. After reaching 5;000 ft. the controller asked us to verify our altitude and I read back 5;000 ft. The controlled returned with 'the MDA is 5;300 in that sector do you have the field in sight?' We had the field in sight but the question led us to believe we descended to the wrong altitude. The controller didn't clarify the altitude at this point and said were cleared for the visual using the RNAV GPS 14 approach plate for guidance.The cause of the event was a miscommunication with ATC and I could have possibly read back a different altitude and thought that 5;000 ft. was what he said instead; after we had set 5000 ft. Also; we were in light to moderate turbulence during the entire flight and it might have caused me to mishear the controller or misread the altitude.I should have asked for clarification from the controller after we had set the altitude in the FMA. From where we were; the altitude of 5000 ft. made sense so it did not cue me to ask for clarification. We had briefed the approach plate as well and the higher rising terrain was on the other side of the field and we determined it would not be a factor for the altitude of 5000 ft. Where we were seemed to coincide with the altitudes on the approach plate as well.

narrative_1: On a relatively calm and clear day at ZZZ1; I departed southbound toward ZZZ. The takeoff was uneventful; I contacted Approach for flight following. Throughout the climb to 9;500 ft.; there was constant light to moderate turbulence; typical for this segment of flight throughout this area. Upon reaching cruise the severity increased to consistent moderate turbulence; again not abnormal for the route of flight; the aircraft was slowed. I reported the ride conditions to Approach; and they stated that a Cessna 208 had reported similar conditions and opted for lower. The airplane began to experience downdrafts; exceeding over 1000 fpm and airspeed fluctuations of +/- 20 knots. I elected to descend to 7;500 ft. based on the ride conditions reported by the aircraft in front of me. At 7;500 ft. I experienced consistent moderate to severe turbulence; with consistent up and downdrafts; accompanied by fluctuations in airspeed. Occasionally; I nearly hit my head on the ceiling of the airplane. I queried [ATC] and they stated that the aircraft had reported a better ride at 6000 ft.; at that time I descended to 6000 ft. At 6000 ft. the ride was much more manageable; and I was able to make it to ZZZ safely. I made the decision that the airplane did in fact fly through severe conditions and required an inspection. I wrote the airplane up and contacted Maintenance Control. The unstable nature of the valley I was flying over and the absence of weather reporting in the valley make it difficult to gauge the ride conditions. I should have slowed the airplane down; and descended to more manageable flight conditions.A solution would have been flying the airplane above the valley to avoid possible severe turbulence. I talked with my pilot supervisor and he advised that flying at 15;500 ft. over the valley is a viable option. This particular route is very abnormal; with respect to mitigating risk. This is a prime example of how quickly things can change when flying. The more we can do to try to mitigate these risks as a whole; the safer it will become.

narrative_1: After a diversion to our planned alternate we had a routine enroute and descent phase. We contacted Tower on about a 10 mile final. We were approximately 5 miles in trail of a B737; and we heard them check in as well. I overheard tower tell them about a Medevac helicopter who was operating to the east of the airport and transiting to the west. Once we were on about a 5 mile final; tower provided us with a traffic call for the same helicopter. The first call we received was traffic at our 10 o'clock and about three miles; and that the traffic had us in sight and was maintaining visual separation. Due to the lights of the city; I did not see the traffic; and it was not yet showing up on our TCAS.Inside of a 4 mile final; at approximately 1200 ft. we received a Traffic Alert for the traffic. On TCAS it showed him at 200 ft. above us and inside a mile. I immediately saw the traffic visually and told the first officer that I had the traffic in sight. Based on the traffic's track and altitude; I very quickly suspected that we might receive an RA. I instructed the first officer to go slightly below the glide slope to increase our separation. Very shortly after that; at 1050 ft. we received a 'DESCEND DESCEND' TCAS Resolution Alert. The First Officer followed the TCAS guidance and I informed ATC. Due to the switch at 1000 ft. to Traffic Alert only we never received a clear of conflict; but we were able to visually identify that we were clear of conflict at about 800 ft. We were one dot low on the glide slope but correcting and all other approach criteria were stable so I quickly asked the First Officer if he felt stable. He responded that he did; so we agreed that we were okay to continue the approach. At our closest point; the helicopter was directly above us and approximately 200 ft. above; leading to a significantly reduced margin of separation.This event was caused by several factors. The helicopter pilot had us in sight and was maintaining visual separation; but in our opinion; the separation provided was not adequate. I was not able to visually identify the traffic until the Traffic Alert occurred; and at that point there was very little we could do to avoid a loss of separation. I do not believe we should have been sequenced by air traffic control to pass directly underneath the medevac's flight path. After landing I communicated my concerns to tower and he said that once the helicopter reported maintaining Visual Separation; he had no further responsibility to separate us. If that is correct; I believe it is a fundamentally unsafe procedure. In this event it led to us receiving a descending RA at 1000 ft. leaving us with very little maneuvering room. I should have made more of an effort to find the traffic prior to receiving a Traffic Alert; but with the city lights it was difficult. This was at the end of a very high workload; 3 hour blocked flight with significant weather; holding; a diversion; and fuel considerations. I believe that this type of event could have been prevented with better planning from air traffic control. There was clearly a difference in expectations between the helicopter pilot and us; and the helicopter pilot may have been comfortable with 200 ft. of separation; but we were not.
narrative_2: We diverted due to weather. On final approach we received a TCAS Resolution Alert due to a medical helicopter crossing the final approach. I was Pilot Flying for the approach. When we received the Traffic Alert; I initially assumed it was an aircraft on a parallel approach. The Pilot Monitoring reported the aircraft in sight. The helicopter had also reported us in sight. Only moments before the Resolution Alert did I realize the aircraft was going to cross directly in front. We received a descending Resolution Alert. I complied with the Resolution Alert. The helicopter passed approximately 200 ft. above. I don't recall ever hearing a clear of conflict call. We descended below 1000 ft. and the TCAS went into Traffic Alert Only mode.A medical helicopter was crossing approximately 3 mile final at approximately 1200 ft. while we were on approach. I was manually flying a challenging approach due to high winds and did not recognize the threat until a few seconds before the Resolution Alert.
synopsis: CRJ900 flight crew reported 200 ft. of separation with a helicopter on approach.

narrative_2: I was given traffic information by ATC while on downwind leg of pattern; a Aircraft X in the pattern ahead and to my left. I said check speed and the PF disengaged the autopilot; reduced power; deployed speed brakes; and leveled off. He had the speed window open and we both failed to monitor the speed window. He is very good about VVM (Verbalize; Verify; Monitor) and not doing something without informing the PM; so I feel I'm just as much responsible for the incident. narrative_2: On the ZZZZZX south of ZZZZZ [Intersection]; we exceeded 250 knots below 10;000 feet.ATC had originally asked us to cross ZZZZZ at 15;000 feet leaving us high for the next restriction (ZZZZZ1 at 8;000 feet and 250 knots). narrative_1: We were navigating between coordinates at FL410 and M.80 assigned.  We received a CPDLC clearance that said; 'Resume normal speed'.  We reviewed the Europe Jeppesen Airway Manual section entitled 'Operations Without an Assigned Speed' to review this relatively new procedure. After agreeing on what it meant we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC at XA:03z via CPDLC 'Present speed .83'.  ATC responded at XA:13z with 'Do you want M.83'.  We responded; 'Received normal speed CLNC and advising our speed is .83'.  At XA:17z ATC sent; 'You may want to read up on that. Resume normal speed means plus or minus mach .01 from cleared mach.'  We immediately changed speed to Mach .81 and replied; 'Roger speed now is .81 requesting M.83' (XA:18z). At XA:19z ATC sent 'Maintain .83M'. All communications were done via CPDLC. The rest of the flight was uneventful.  We disagree with the controller's interpretation of the 'Resume normal speed' clearance and request clarification from the company. Page 668 of the Jeppesen Airway Manual (Europe) says; 'If the aircraft then receives RESUME NORMAL SPEED (via CPDLC or Voice); the flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However; the flight crew shall advise ATC if; as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message; they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed.'  Furthermore; in the operational example given on page 688 it says; '...message RESUME NORMAL SPEED will be sent.  The flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However; the flight crew shall advise ATC if; as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message; they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed. In this case; with a previously assigned speed of .81; they must inform ATC if the flight either slows to M.79 or less or speeds up to M.83 or more.'  Finally; in the North America Jeppesen Airway Manual it says; ' When adherence to an assigned 'MACH' setting is no longer required; pilots will receive a controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) message to 'RESUME NORMAL SPEED;' at which point the flight crew can continue at their cost index. Refer to aeronautical information circular (AIC) 1/20 Operations Without an Assigned Fixed Speed (OWAFS) in the North Atlantic for more details.'  In looking at the ICAO NAT OPS Bulletin (2019_001); the text mimics what is published in the Jeppesen Airway Manual. In conclusion; I believe we were in full compliance with the 'Resume normal speed' clearance when we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC but since the controller has a different understanding of the situation I would like to get clarification from the company.

narrative_1: I am a contract pilot and an on-call simulator instructor on the various Falcon EASy airplanes. The PIC is an experienced large airplane pilot. His current experiences are on numerous types of Boeings; etc. He became the manager/pilot of the subject -900EASy and has roughly 6 flights with this aircraft; most with me. His type training was about 3 months ago and he did not fly the airplane until roughly 1.5-2.0 months after his check ride (guesstimate). I have been providing SIC support (until the other full-time pilot can accomplish his type training) as well as IOE on the airplane and especially on the EASy avionics. The pilot's 'airliner avionics' background has generated system misunderstandings that I have corrected. This includes incorrect use of Flight Guidance selection choices. While arriving on the STAR into ZZZ we were advised to 'descend via the STAR'. The Captain highly prefers to use VNAV for virtually all climbs and descents and as he was selecting such I was reprogramming our waypoints for altitude crossings. The Captain then questioned me as to 'how best to set up the VNAV function'. I explained various ways to do so; i.e. VNAV versus minimum altitude to select; using the vertical profile 'laser pointer' to start the descent or to use for constant descent without stair-stepping through crossing altitudes; how to change the descent angle utilized on the FMS avionics page; etc. However; after some time I noticed that the VNAV was not capturing and that the 'laser pointer' was moving away from the target setting; i.e. waypoint selected for crossing. This happened a few times. I even showed him how to do a 'Direct Vertical Descend To' but it also did not work. The Captain was complaining about the EASy system compared to the Boeings he flies and couldn't understand why it was not capturing. During this time I was acquiring the ATIS and setting up for the approach to be utilized. However; when I once again noted that we were still not descending correctly I stopped doing my functions and spent more time analyzing the situation. That is when I noticed that the airplane was west of the intended course (I would guess about 4-5 miles). I then informed him that somehow he had lost LNAV guidance. As such; the VNAV would not be correct. Although he asked me to now give him direct to the waypoint I told him he instead needed to rejoin the arrival and advised him to use HDG (heading) or TRCK (track) to perform a turn back to rejoin. He said he understood but I noticed his confusion and delay in doing so. I again advised him that he needed to get back on course and almost simultaneously ATC noticed our discrepancy. Because of our course deviation we did not descend accordingly. As such; ATC gave us a direct to ZZZZZ and cross at 10;000. I performed the 'direct to' and advised the Captain to start an immediate descent which he slowly did; however; the eventual angle was high and as such the airspeed increased. He complained about the increasing speed and I told him that he needs full airbrakes to check the speed increase (twice). He looked confused and delayed the extension of the airbrakes until the speed had already climbed; i.e. he now had to reduce the speed he had allowed to increase during the initial descend maneuver. Therefore; we exceeded the 250 knots below 10;000 feet for roughly 600-700 feet (I think we were back at 250 before 9;300 ft.) The remainder of the flight was uneventful. I should note that during a post debrief the Captain was noting how only one person should be touching the guidance panel. He was; in my opinion; somewhat deflecting responsibility for the loss of the LNAV function (after I asked him if he knew how we lost LNAV guidance). However; I did not manipulate the panel. I pointed to what and where he needed to go for his choice of modes. This is especially true during the initial mistake. Although I cannot guarantee my thought I think that the Captain inadvertently disconnected LNAV after passingZZZZZ1 while we were setting up for the descent. He has previously chosen the wrong button before; e.g. he once switched guidance to the non-flying pilot during his attempt at setting-up another choice. At that time I saw his action and corrected him immediately (that time I did change the setting myself). It was in a very high workload moment and I did not have the time then to explain to him what he had done. In that situation I needed to get the guidance back to the pilot flying which necessitated a minimum of three button selections. After a little time; and after I had completed what I was doing as the SIC; I attempted to explain what he had done but prior to such he said he understood his mistake so I did not delve deeper into it. Since aircraft traffic in the ZZZ area was light there was no deviations and ATC did not 'appear upset'. However; I felt it important to write this ASRS Report. This Captain is very confident of his methods (he is very experienced) and strives to be as efficient as possible. He chooses to carry the minimum fuel required for a trip; always flies at Long Range Cruise power setting; requests as many short cuts as possible; and wishes to start the airplane moving as quickly as possible after engine starts. As such; he has often questioned me in relation to after start tests that need to be performed for each flight versus those that only need to be performed once a day; or maybe even once a week. He does not like sitting with engines running. Therefore; we are sometimes somewhat in a hurry. Being the SIC and as a contract pilot I have acquiesced to his overall style as it is not illegal or unsafe; although it is not the method I prefer. For a pilot new to an airplane I would recommend that the pilot 'go slow' and diligently learn the process of the new airplane but a pilot's prior experiences can alter that process. This is especially true when the pilot has a vast (many years) experience flying numerous large airplanes worldwide. I have suggested that this Captain fly as the SIC for a bit to truly learn the airplane but he noted that during his training he only got experience in the left seat. His comment was that he wants to become familiar with the left seat before trying the right seat. As the SIC can be busy it is hard for an experienced pilot (in a particular airplane) in that role to provide guidance to an inexperienced pilot (in a particular airplane) while doing both instruction; IOE overview; and normal duties simultaneously. My recommendation is that regardless of experience that a pilot 'to a new airplane' be limited to the SIC duties for a minimum of 5 flights (segments; not hours) before transitioning to the left seat. What is required is the 'muscle and mental memory' performing the numerous tasks associated with the various sections of a flight.

We were getting bumped around pretty good by now; full continuous moderate turbulence. It was at that moment when the autopilot was capturing the altitude that the upset occurred. The aircraft was rocked to a 45 to 50 degree left bank and a sinking drop occurred similar to what you would receive in an airliner if you ever have hit an air pocket. This exceeded the limits of the autopilot and it kicked off. I took over manually to right the airplane and that is when we received what I would call a severe bump which led to the second upset that did the same thing; left bank to 45 to 50 degrees and a pitch downward.  I was already in the process of advancing power from the first upset but this time I went to full thrust; TOGA power if you will; to initiate the unusual attitude recovery.  I was aggressive in the recovery; put some G on the aircraft; airspeed bled down from 250 to about 180 or 190 at that moment which is still a safe flying airspeed in our type aircraft; well above stall.  I traded airspeed for altitude to expedite the recovery.  We recovered to altitude shortly after.This all happened so quickly.
