About 15 seconds later; tower called me up again; asking 'Aircraft X - extend it out a little bit; actually just follow behind and I'll call your base you will have to follow a jet behind on final'. I read back and confirmed.About 30 seconds later; tower called me up again; 'Aircraft X just so I don't get you too far from the field; make a left 360'. I read back the instruction and began my left 360. At this point; I was already thinking about Aircraft Y as I was planning on how I would get back on the downwind and line up behind them. I believe Aircraft Y was just about to finish its right 270 as I was about 90 degrees into my 360. I was able to spot and track the plane on Foreflight with Sentry; but since I had to make a 360 I lost visual when I initiated my turn. Tower; likely receiving a traffic alert called the other plane to make them aware of me: 'Aircraft X about a mile south making a left 360 - he has you in sight'. I do not think he asked them to confirm that they had me in sight and I can't tell from the live-ATC recording whether they read it back. The added statement 'he has you in sight' was extremely dangerous and could have been fatal. Yes; I had the traffic in sight when I was heading toward it and planning to get behind them; but once I started my left 360 there was no way of maintaining a visual with the other plane since I was now heading the opposite direction. I immediately recognized the potential conflict and started looking both outside the plane and on Foreflight trying to spot and track the other plane's relative position. The other plane did not make a 270 turn; but instead kept turning toward the airport/runway i.e. cutting into my path.As I was about 270 degrees into my 360 turn tower called 'Aircraft X - as you are coming out of that 360 turn do you still have Aircraft Y in sight?'At this point; I was already banking hard left in a steep turn trying to pull away from the converging traffic that I saw coming closer toward me. Turning right was not an option as it would have put me in the middle of final with jets arriving. I do not think the other plane confirmed whether or not they had me in sight. If they did; they flew way too close to me for my comfort and should have initiated an avoidance maneuver. In response to tower's question I responded 'Aircraft X unable' because I had to focus on flying the airplane away from the other traffic. We then passed by each other with much less separation than I feel comfortable. The other plane heading toward the runway; and me pulling hard left to the North-West; initiating a climb up to gain altitude. It is hard to tell exactly but horizontal distance could have been less than 500 feet Vertical distance was virtually the same. It happened very quickly. If I had not realized the potential conflict and mitigated by tracking on foreflight and pulling hard left this could have been a really really bad situation. The biggest mistake here; in my opinion; was ATC communicating to the other plane that I had them in sight AFTER I started my 360. There is no way one can maintain visual during such a maneuver while also flying safely and ATC shouldunder no circumstances make that statement. I also think that having two planes completing maneuvers in a way where their exit paths can conflict (right 270 and left 360) in close proximity should be prohibited.There were multiple safer options here. Aircraft Y could have flown a proper base rather than cutting it short onto final. I could have been asked to fly west; or I could have been asked to fly another 360 right after the first one. The fact that ATC changed its instructions relative to how I should fly behind/around the other traffic 3 times in a minute indicates to me that they were not planning ahead but rather responding to/running behind.In the future; I will call out if ATC tells other people that I have them in sight when I don't (i.e. after starting my left 360). I am also surprised nobody (tower/the other plane) complained about how close this was. I am glad to be back on the ground.  I hope this helps keep other people safe in the future!
synopsis: GA pilot reported experiencing a NMAC that resulted from ATC sequencing 3 aircraft for landing by using 270- and 360-turns.

Dispatch was unaware that this stub flight was not flying the amended flight plan they sent us. When I; as the relief pilot; arrived from my break on the flight deck I noticed the erroneous flight progress forms and notified Dispatch who then sent us the revised flight plan. Dispatch was unaware that we were back on our original PACOTS routing. This was accomplished 2+45 into the flight. However if I had not done this it would not have gotten done as the FO refused to contact Dispatch to clear up the confusion. please advise. The First Officer refused input from both the Captain and myself; the relief pilot; to contact Dispatch and get them in the loop regarding discrepancies from filed flights from amended ones. Since the only discrepancy between the flight plans was at the end of the flight; we opted to depart. narrative_1: Getting radar vectors to intercept the final approach course to Runway 34L RNO;  ATC instructed us to fly direct to SPOON at 11;000 ft and intercept the localizer. Upon overflying SPOON; the GPS commanded an aggressive; yet smooth; right turn to final. Once on final; we intercepted the localizer and descended on the glide path while observing the altitude restrictions at APIME; WAGGE; and EPOSE. The FO (First Officer) and I were fully 'dialed in' for this approach as we had briefed the procedure; identified the surrounding terrain; and associated threats. Landed uneventfully. Three days later I was advised ATC identified our airplane as one that lost acceptable separation with terrain during our approach. The FO was making his first trip to RNO and I had only been to RNO a few times in at least a few years. We were initially planning to fly an approach to the south until ATC told us to expect one to Runway 34L. The routing to SPOON put us at (approx.) 90 degrees to the final approach course with (from memory) an unreliable localizer signal at D24.6. That large angle and our reluctance to use the localizer so far from the field forced us into using the GPS which caused an overfly situation; and thus; and overshoot of the final approach course. I think getting a heading to intercept the final approach course inside SPOON and at a lesser angle would alleviate the overshoot possibility and the resulting loss of separation.

During the descent to 2;000 MSL; I briefly looked up at the Pressurization Control Panel to monitor the PNF progress in controlling the cabin pressure; I noted the cabin pressure was finally close to the aircraft's actual altitude. I directed the PNF to select 'RAM AIR' ON.  That action stabilized the cabin for landing. ATC called to confirm our 2;000 feet clearance limit and I realized that the aircraft did not level off at 2;000 feet and the autopilot was not engaged. I acknowledged our clearance to ATC; manually flew the plane from 1;700 feet to 2;000 feet and reengaged to Autopilot. Since the cabin pressure was finally under control; an uneventful approach and landing were completed. Due to the distraction of the cabin pressure control issues; as PF I briefly failed to monitor the aircraft flight profile. Since I had tasked the PNF to attempt to stabilize the cabin pressure; I take full responsibility for failing to continuously monitor the aircraft flight profile.No matter what cockpit distractions occur; it is incumbent upon the PF to continuously monitor the aircraft flight profile. Aircraft X subsequently continued a left turn towards ZZZ1 and entered a 2;500' MVA at his assigned altitude of 2;000'.  The trainee was aware of the incident almost immediately. He reported that he was starting a climb to 7;000 feet.One minute after he started his climb; at XA:32Z; I picked up a primary target in the area the pilot reported. I tried to verify the position of the primary target; but the pilot just responded that he was showing zero oil pressure and having electrical issues. As he was saying this; the data block correlated to the code and I radar identified Aircraft X and verified his location. My standard practice; something that I did less than ten minutes prior; is to radar identify; verify location and altitude; and give altimeter. I do it every time; and in that order. When I radar identified Aircraft X; there was no Mode C data; so I asked him to report his altitude. He reported that he was climbing to 7;000 feet and asked for help to get into ZZZ; he was showing zero on his oil pressure. I didn't circle back to the altimeter at this time.I issued Aircraft X a heading to set him up for a pattern into ZZZ. If his engine was about to quit; I wanted him lined up for an airport; not guessing what was below him. I told the CIC I was working a special aircraft; and the OM was quickly in the area. I didn't feel it was in good judgement to add on to the pilot's stress level by pointing out that he was experiencing an urgent situation. It was being handled as such.He asked as he rolled out if he was on the correct heading. I advised that he was 20 degrees off course; and that he should correct. He told me he was using his backup compass; due to electrical failure. That information made a lot of sense at that moment. The backup compass is a magnetic compass. It's one that bounces around as you turn it. The magnetic compass will continue to turn past the heading and then bounce back and correct as the airplane levels off and the compass stabilizes. This is something that an IFR rated pilot would be more knowledgeable about. No gyro turns; or turns with only the backup compass were part of my IFR certificate training. Due to this; I decided to give him small turns that would create an arc to final; and help him maintain better control and orientation.I told him to descend to 5;000 ft. and that I should still have radar contact at that altitude. He responded that believed he'd be able to poke through. I knew it would be minimal conditions; I still believed getting the aircraft set up for a runway was the safest places. As I gave him a turn to the left he stated that he was going to get into the clouds. I asked if he and the aircraft were IFR qualified. He said they were not. I asked if he could maintain VFR conditions. It sounded like he was trying; but didn't seem sure that he would.I told Aircraft X that he could continue down to 4;000 feet and gave him a heading to get him turned more toward the airport. About that time at XA:39Z; just eleven minutes into the situation; an aircraft inbound for ZZZ1 checked on. I issued the ZZZ1 altimeter. This aircraft would end up being held out for the [situation]. I then told Aircraft X he could descend at his discretion to 3;900 feet; but that was the minimum enroute altitude in the area; and the lowest I was comfortable advising him. He said he was starting to poke through at 4;100 feet. I gave him the position and distance of ZZZ1. He responded that he could see some ground.I had him continue his gradual left turn but saw a much more aggressive turn on the radar. I asked if he was circling down to stay in VFR conditions. He said he saw bases at 3;800 feet and it was an unintentional 360. Based on what the radar showed; it was not a controlled maneuver; and probably resulted from an unusual attitude due to spatial disorientation. I asked him to regain level flight; as to maintain control of the aircraft and not get into another unusual attitude. I asked him his altitude; he responded 3;680 [feet]. In the clouds a turn can make your body feel like you are descending; and a climb can make your body think you are turning. A more abrupt climb or turn only magnifies this effect. At XA:43Z as I maintained focus on keeping the pilot's wings level; I offered the option of climbing back up into VFR conditions. He was in favor of the idea. He added that the engine had been running fine; and believed the zero oil pressure reading to be due to electrical issue; not engine issues. He said the engine was running fine now; no longer a concern. I told him that we believed it to be clear in ZZZ2; ZZZ3; and ZZZ4. He said that sounds nice. I wanted to get him into ZZZ3 if it was in fact clear. It was much closer; and based on his workload; fatigue due to stress; and equipment issues; I wanted him in the air the least amount of time possible. I was focused on getting Aircraft X oriented and into VMC.I told him to fly his present heading and start a climb; advising that there was no traffic ahead. He responded that he was having trouble keeping his wings level. I advised back to straight and level and asked his altitude. I should have advised him to focus on the instruments over his own sensations; but I did not think of it at the time.He said he was at 4;020 feet. Aircraft X then responded; he pulled into a stall; but was starting back up. I advised him to take it slow. At that point Aircraft Y verified ZZZ2 to be clear. I asked if Aircraft X was staying level. He said yes; 5;000 feet and seeing sunlight. I saw another turn on radar and had him level his wings once again. In my experience; it was best to remind him that he could exhale. He still needed to have the ability to fly the rest of his flight with electrical issues. I also offered him the opportunity to request an alternate airport. He had equipment that most likely needed to be repaired or replaced. I didn't want to send him somewhere that he'd get stuck. Many communications are being missed in the last months because ATC are covering too many sectors. narrative_2: Flight was left high on the ZZZZZ Arrival.   ATIS had us landing on [Runway] XXR. narrative_1: Aircraft X was vectored to their final approach course approximately 3 to 4 miles in trail of a preceding Aircraft Y. We were VFR conditions but had low ceilings hovering around 1;000 feet. Aircraft weren't coming out of the clouds until a 1 to 2 mile final. When Aircraft X joined the approach they has an absurdly high overtake speed with the Aircraft Y in front of them of 80 plus knots. There was no way separation was ever going to be maintained. When the realization set in of what was happening Local Control issued instructions to cancel the approach and to climb to 3000 feet and to turn 20 degrees to the left.  I began coordination with Departure Control for a handoff with vectors to bring the aircraft back around for another approach. In the meantime Aircraft X advised Local Control that they were minimum fuel and were continuing the approach. Local Control advised me of this; so I canceled the coordination; and redirected my attention to an aircraft awaiting clearance. Then Local Control advised me that Aircraft X was indeed going around with the 20 degree left turn; and 3000 foot altitude assignment. Traffic was light; so I instructed Local Control to climb Aircraft X to 6000 feet and issue a turn to get them into the dispersal area as per our joint agreement. I again initiated coordination with Departure Control for the handoff; with Aircraft X climbing to 6000 feet and on a 100 or 105 heading.Then I came back to the aircraft on Clearance Delivery and had them read back their clearance. During the read back; Departure was trying to call me and say that Aircraft X needed to climb immediately for an aircraft that was departing southeast bound off a satellite airport. I responded that the altitude had been issued and would find out why Aircraft X stopped their climb at 3000 feet. I relayed the information to Local Control as I was receiving it.  Local Control told me that Aircraft X would not accept the climb due to their minimum fuel situation; which I relayed back to Departure. Departure Control requested we ship Aircraft X to them; so that they could maintain separation with the traffic departing the satellite airport which I relayed to Local. Local was able to get Aircraft X to climb to 4;000 feet before shipping them. There was a loss of lateral separation on final approach; but there may have been altitude separation; although I am not sure about that. The problem is that we are struggling with spacing issues on final and even have a collaborative work group established with Approach to resolve these problems. Approach is continually handing Tower these overtakes;  and less than coordinated arrival spacing for departure gaps; but Tower is always held accountable for the consequences of each event. This is the standard here at  even though the separation problem originates with the Approach Controller. Even our local management tends to initially stand behind Approach and their actions while pointing their fingers at the Tower controllers trying to tell us that what we did was incorrect; even though we are only trying our best to prevent an separation error from occurring or getting worse.  Standardize spacing requirements here at 3 miles or required and coordinated arrival spacing distances and never transfer communications of aircraft on final until there is less than a 30 knot overtake speed. In other words; follow the guidance in the 7110.65 and ensure separation before transferring communications to another controller. And on top of this; performance management to ensure controllers are being held accountable to the basic standards.
synopsis: A Tower Controller reported they coordinated a go around for an aircraft with Departure Control but the aircraft did not climb to the assigned altitude resulting in a loss of prescribed separation.

narrative_1: Just after completing a climb to 12;000 ft in an attempt to get above an icing layer; the company issued iPad mount fell off the windscreen on to the floor. Initially; I reacted to this by reaching down to pick it up; but simultaneously noticed the G600 displayed a GPS failure indication on the moving map side of the screen. At the same time TAWS (terrain awareness and warning system) gave an aural alert 'TAWS NOT AVAILABLE'. There were no additional audible alerts or visual annunciations. I initially thought this was simply a GPS signal failure and was starting to react accordingly; I then observed that the aircraft had entered a descending turn and immediately reacted with an unusual attitude in IMC recovery procedure. Given that the aircraft was in continuous light turbulence; in the clouds; at night; I was momentarily completely focused on ensuring the aircraft remained in a controlled attitude. A few moments latter I began taking stock of what I did and did not have. I observed the GMX200 screen off; GNS530 screen off; the primary GTX330 was off; and the autopilot was off. The G600 was giving associated GPS/AHRS and GAD43 failures. There were no other annunciations on the primary panel; and no audible alerts. My next focus was to re-establish navigation to my next known waypoint; the ZZZ VOR. I had previously tuned the ZZZ VOR into the NAV1 and NAV2; so I had manual navigation and DME via NAV2. Since the GNS430 and secondary GTX330 appeared operable; I immediately squawked 7600 as I had been out of contact with ZZZ1 Center (which was on COM1) and had obviously deviated heading/altitude at the beginning of the incident a few moments earlier. Not knowing what was happening to cause these failures and what might be failing next; setting the squawk may at the very least alert Center that I am having a problem. I also needed a few moments to sort out which frequency I needed to be on; as at this point the stress level was high enough I could not remember the frequency. I had to retrieve the iPad which was still on the floor in order to look at the chart screen for the frequency. Once back in contact with ZZZ1 Center I described the situation as best I could: some kind of electrical and/or communication failure as most of my avionics were now off. I elected for a diversion to ZZZ; now about 17nm away; and worry about troubleshooting the problem on the ground rather in the air in IMC at night. I was given vectors for a visual approach and landed without further incident.Having time to analyze the situation; and noting after landing/parking that the Avionics 1 & 2 were able to be switch back on; I conclude that the root cause of the systems associated with Avionics Bus 1 failing was from the iPad mount falling off the windscreen and hitting the switch on the way down. In personal reflection; I can recognize the irony that simply reaching over to check the avionics switches would have likely resolved the issue. But; the totality of the circumstances I had been suddenly faced with: 'an unexpected flight attitude deviation following an otherwise innocuous distraction; an initial observation of having a GPS signal failure'. Normally a failure of the GNS530/430; even if the failure was a complete loss of the entire unit; would not have resulted in the loss of the autopilot modes. Typically any normal failure of the autopilot is also accompanied by an audible alert. I had no immediate indication that the autopilot was off until observing the aircraft starting a descending turn. This precipitated the human factor contribution to the scenario of dealing with an otherwise unexplainable loss of avionics and uncommanded attitude deviation and no indication to which trained emergency checklist actions would be a prudent course of action. Overall troubleshooting based on system knowledge is a higher level brain function and at the time I did not have the luxury of 'stepping back' to think what might be going wrong. All that to say; there are no checklists specifically for an avionics failure (such as the switch some how getting turned off) or even what to do if the GPS fails. The assumed reactions remain in the realm of pilot knowledge and ability to troubleshoot the problem in lieu of following a checklist... in all likelihood with the assumption that the autopilot is still functional. This isn't a suggestion that we make a new checklist item; but rather the addition of random failure modes such as this during training to either establish situational memory or reinforce what to do if you don't know what to do. Finally; the root culprit of the situation... the iPad mount. This has been an ongoing 'issue' that has been simply tolerated by Company pilots. It hasn't been reported likely because we didn't think it was a big problem; would have never imagined it would lead to any problem; or have not been explicitly told that it is a problem if it occurs. There is also the ongoing back and forth with pilots who do not like having the mount and will remove it from the windscreen. The result is the mount ends up on the floor; getting dirty and damaged to the point that many of the suction cups do not effectively stay on the windscreen. In fact; in talking with another co-worker I discovered that this exact scenario happened to him during an AM departure a few weeks earlier and had hit both Avionics 1 & 2 switches. Since he saw it (and had the benefit of being VFR during the day) he just turned the switches back on and remounted the iPad. It has been my observation the suction cups seem to most frequently fail when climbing into colder temperatures; but this is not always the case. At this point; I believe it is safe to say that the current mounting system does not work... either by nature of system or as a result of the poor care and handling it as received over the past year or so. I will have to admit; the iPad mount coming off is something that I have observed and didn't report... and frankly should have reported and made a big stink over sooner. But I am now: at this point I do not believe the current iPad mounting system to be either effective nor safe.
synopsis: Pilot reported iPAD falling out of it's mount; striking the Avionics Bus 1 and 2 switches; causing failures of most avionics and communication systems.

Approach had us at 190 knots departing DSNEE; and we were expecting the visual to runway 20R. We had gone to flaps 2 configuration. We were handed off late to the final controller; and when we switched over we heard a company call sign with nearly identical numeric as ours; cleared for the RNAV (RNP) Z runway 20R. We heard the other aircraft read back the clearance; we knew a VERY similar call sign was on frequency. We thought we might be cleared for the same approach. We checked in and asked if we were going to get the RNAV approach; and the controller said no; we were going to get a visual unless we asked for the approach. Shortly after; the controller cleared an aircraft to descend to 3000'; but neither of us were sure that it was our call sign. The First Officer (FO) attempted to clarify; but the controller was very busy and talking nonstop. We flew a few more miles; and before we could clarify he repeated the clearance to descend to 3000' and asked if we had the airport in sight. We called the airport; and said we were high. He cleared us to fly through final approach course and intercept from the right. FO read back the clearance; and we both agreed it was going to be tight. I immediately called for gear down and got the flaps to full; I also used the speed brakes as long as safely practical. We switched over to tower control; and I made the glideslope at approx. 1400' AGL; but we were still 40kts fast. I told the FO we were going to do a 'Soft Go'. At 1000' AGL I called for 'Go Around; Takeoff/around (TOGA)' and advanced the thrust levers to TOGA. I then called 'climb' as I brought the thrust levers back to what I thought was the climb position; but was actually the Maximum Continuous Thrust (MCT) detent. The tower initially held us to 2000'; so I reduced our climb rate - we were accelerating rapidly. As we cleaned up and were cleared to 3000'; the FO recognized that we were in MCT detent and brought it to my attention. By then we were clean and rapidly approaching 250 KIAS. I brought the thrust levers back to idle as we passed 260; and we saw a maximum speed of about 280 before we began to slow down again. I selected speed mode and set 220 KIAS; positioned the thrust levers in the climb detent and re-engaged auto thrust. We slowed and turned back into a right downwind for an uneventful visual approach and landing at SNA.Causes(1)	Late clearance to descend. SNA is challenging even when on a normal profile; and a few miles made all the difference.(2)	Task saturation. The L.A basin is one of the busiest airspaces in the world. Two Traffic Alerts and nonstop chatter from the approach controller indicated that he was task saturated; as well.(3)	Call sign confusion. The scheduling shop should never have had two call signs separated by one digit arriving at the same airport at the same time.(4)	Approach expectations. We were going to do a visual; and changed our setup and expectations when we heard preceding traffic approach clearance.(5)	Fatigue. Our FAR 117 duty day limit was 10 hours. We had been awake since 3.5 hours earlier to make sign-in; and were at 9:00 of our 10:00 limit when we arrived at SNA. When we knew we were too high to likely make a successful approach; we could have asked for a vector and more time/distance to descend. Flight scheduling needs to de-conflict call signs so very similar ones are not scheduled to arrive at the same airport at the same time. The ATC controllers seemed very busy; perhaps a few more controllers on-shift would help divide the workload better. Crew scheduling could alleviate fatigue factors by avoiding sequence builds that have crews flying into airports at the back end of their duty periods that are known to present unusual challenges (even if they aren't officially 'special qualification' airports).
synopsis: Airbus First officer reported a go-around caused by late clearance to descend and confusion caused by a similar call sign for an aircraft preceding them.

narrative_1: I wanted to take a few minutes to relate to you my personal experiences during the events that transpired.  We were at the tail end of a lengthy four day trip; with the usual holiday related challenges; weather; maintenance; crew-placarding; lengthy sit times; de-icing etc. On the third day of the trip; we were waiting in line for departure on [Runway] XXL at ZZZ; when the tower informed us that the operation was shut down for a 'deep-cleaning' at ZZZ1 Center.  Having personally experienced the same the same scenario last year when both the ZZZ2 Tower and ground were shut down for a COVID spread throughout their Tower; it didn't take long for us to figure out the reason for the closure.Like everyone one else in our situation; we opened up the FOM and began compliance with the notification processes for the passengers; the Flight Attendants; and ZZZ Ops. My First Officer (FO) and I immediately began working the 14 hour duty day issue; (FO A was my second FO during the course of the trip; and he had a less restrictive duty day constraint than I did).  After nearly two hours at the hold short line; we began the process of finding a gate; with the intent to avoid the prospective government fines levied for lengthy delays. It was the usual chaos; with ZZZ Ops being overwhelmed by this unforeseen event.  As we approach the two hour FOM deadline for locating a gate; we were assigned DXX via ACARS.  While taxiing to the gate; we made multiple attempts to get guidance from Ops; Ramp; Dispatch; etc.; to see what the intent was for the passengers; my crew; and the aircraft. We were unable to get any specific guidance. Following our arrival at the gate; an Agent opened the main door; and told us that the flight would be cancelled. As directed by the agent; the passengers disembarked with their bags. Since we had seen no changes to our crew schedule; nor had we received any kind of communication from crew tracking; we assumed that the agent was correct regarding the cancellation; and as such; we began reviewing our required duty time obligations. Absent any further guidance; we subsequently put the aircraft 'to bed;' and once again we attempted to contact crew tracking; (no luck there).  Rather than exit into the terminal; we elected to continue to wait on the aircraft.After 20 minutes or so; a new Agent came down the bridge; and asked me if we were ready to board the aircraft. Needless to say; I was a bit astonished.  I asked her what the plan was; and she said that we were going to resume the flight to ZZZ3; ASAP.  I reminded her that the airspace was still closed; and that we had not received any contact from either dispatch or tracking; regarding an updated release; and that we would need additional fuel; lavatory/water service; and a resupply of the delay rations that the Flight Attendants had used for the passengers during our time spent waiting on the taxiway. I also told her that both of us; along with two of the Flight Attendants had duty-time issues that we have to calculate and resolve before departure.  She promptly replied and asked me; 'Captain are you refusing to board the aircraft?'I immediately realized that this was the standard pass-the buck/assign the delay language; that some Agents use in an attempt to intimidate Pilots. I took several deep breaths; before I stated to her in no uncertain terms; that we would need to at least begin to address the aforementioned issues; before we would be comfortable boarding the aircraft again.  Her reply was; 'Captain; are you refusing to board the aircraft?'  I answered that until we get some of these issues resolved; yes.  What was clear to myself; my FO and the number one Flight Attendant; is that this was clearly an attempt at pilot-pushing. [In my opinion]; this Agent had one concern; and that was to make sure that these passengers would become someone else's problem; (namely ours).Long story short; and after significant efforts by all involved; we reconstituted the flight and determined that without further lengthy ground delays that we would likely arrive in ZZZ3 within our respective 14 hour duty day window. We then performed our usual checklists; flows; refueling; new clearance etc.After push-back; start and taxi instructions were received; I made my first mistake of the flight; and turned in the direct opposite direction of ground's instructions on the taxi clearance. It was at this point that I realized I was a lot more tired than I thought.  My FO and I discussed this; and we agreed that though we were both somewhat tired; it was safe to proceed; and that we should just take extra time and precautions going forward.Mistake number two on my part was that when ATC changed our departure STAR; we briefed it at the gate; had it up on our iPads; but I had failed to enter it in the MCDU. After wheels up; ATC gave us direct-to clearance to a fix that wasn't on the legs page. My FO quickly realized that I hadn't entered the new departure STAR; and he rapidly remedied it on the MCDU. I was mad at myself for making this series of unprecedented and inexplicable mistakes. Those mistakes continued as we descended on the type of complex STAR with a series of 'at or above' altitude constraints; that confounds the logic on some of the older 'Basic' airplanes.Needless to say; we landed safely in ZZZ3 later that evening. After block-in; I determined that I was within my duty legality; by 20 minutes or so. It had been a very long day.  We had departed ZZZ4 that morning before the sun had risen; and we had left the gate at ZZZ for the second time; well after the sun had set. In summary; I had made many embarrassing operational mistakes during the course of the last leg; beginning with my pre-flight; push back; all the way through the descent into ZZZ3.  The only explanation for my numerous mistakes was fatigue. In short; I will never; ever; again allow the 'system' to push to me beyond my own personal safety limits. I will take my First Officers counsel more seriously when it comes to considering just how tired we are.Additional factors include that when you consider the cumulative effects of four and five day trips on us; along with a 14 hour duty period; it can be well beyond the average pilot's limitations to safely operate.  And while I don't blame the agent personally; (like everyone else; she was just doing the job in the manner that she was trained); and like everyone else she's just under time pressure.  As time has gone by at our company; it has become clear to me; that the safety culture at the top of this airline; is in many respects; mostly honored and kept in place; by those who of us; who are at the pointy end of the spear.In retrospect; the main causal factor was fatigue due to a lengthy delay.Two suggestions.  The first is that [in my opinion]; we need to take into account the cumulative effect of a lengthy four and five day trip on pilot fatigue.  The other issue is Gate Agent conduct and verbiage regarding flight Ops as it regards to boarding the passengers.
synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported several operational errors occurring after a long ground delay long due to an 'ATC Zero' event.

narrative_1: On route to the airport the First Officer's Multi Function display failed. We decided to continue destination airport because it was not required equipment. Then we were informed the weather at the airport was deteriorating unexpectedly. We completed all the required tasks and checklist before the we were cleared for the approach. On approach we realized that we were too high and our descent profile was going to be unacceptable for a stable approach. Around 11;000 ft. the Captain called for the Missed Approach. We executed the Missed Approach with no issues and cleaned up the aircraft and started climbing to the missed approach altitude. We were at the missed approach altitude and Captain called for the auto pilot on. During this time there was a bit of confusion and the right turn and swapping the navigation displays and setting the new course for the back course was slow to be executed. We turned to the heading too slow and never intercepted the back course. Once we figured out that we didn't intercept the back course we had the Course Deviation Indicator full-scale deflection. ATC gave us a new altitude and a new heading to start the restart the approach. We got vectored around to the Initial Approach Fix to restart the approach and completed the second approach stabilized without any issues. Failure to comply with the approach profile and the missed approach profile.
narrative_2: I neglected to call for the First Officer to start our descent. The First Officer noticed my mistake; but by this time we were very high. My initial reaction was to deploy the boards and steepen the descent in an attempt to get back on profile; however I quickly realized it wasn't going to work and we were unstabilized. I called for a missed approach when we were at roughly 11;000 ft.  Because we went missed early; I called for the autopilot on once we reached the published missed approach altitude of 14;200 ft. This caused confusion as to who should complete the tasks of spinning the heading knob to the 300 heading; swapping the RTU's; and setting the course to 303. I decided to have the First Officer complete these to stay as on-profile as possible. The first two tasks; the 300 heading and swapping the RTU's; were completed however the task of setting the 303 course was not. This led to ATC querying us about our progress on the missed approach and soon after issuing an altitude alert with an instruction to climb to 15;000 ft. By the time we figured out our mistake we were showing full-scale deflection on the Course Deviation Indicator. In addition to not setting the course; I made the mistake of accelerating to 200 kts. and calling climb sequence once level at 14;200 ft. instead of waiting until outbound per the profile. I should also add that the First Officer MFD failed enroute and this most likely caused a reduction in situational awareness throughout the rest of the flight. Failure to comply with the LOC/DME 15 approach profile; especially the missed approach segment.

narrative_1: I was using a safety pilot and view limiting device to log instrument approaches to regain IFR currency. I was on climbout/missed approach from a low approach to a practice ILS X at ZZZ. I was told to by the Tower to 'proceed on course' after having previously told the Approach Controller I was headed next to ZZZ1 for the next approach. I was switched to ZZZ Approach at about 1;800 feet MSL on climbout and reported 1;900 feet for 3;000 feet direct ZZZ1. I was told 'Radar contact' and nothing else specifically.On climbout I was trying to set up my Garmin 430W for the next approach; and get a new program on the iPad (Foreflight vs. Garmim pilot I had previously used) to post the selected approach for ZZZ1 on the map. I had trouble with my glasses fogging up due to wearing a COVID mask in the plane and was experiencing updrafts/turbulence. The time to 3;000 feet was shorter than expected and due to the above distractions; I did not notice I was passing through 3;000 feet until I hit 3;250 feet at which point I reduced power and pushed the nose down. I was back to 3;000 feet within 15 seconds. I heard nothing from ATC regarding this; probably due to being VFR and no altitude restriction issued by ATC. I was able to verify all audio and events/altitudes due to a GoPro running to capture the flight.While I was VFR and there was no traffic nearby; if this was IFR; I would have had the same challenges and it would most likely been an altitude bust. There needs to be the same discipline applied to 'practice' instrument work as there is during the real thing in IMC; or the bad habits and distractions you allow during practice will seep into operations in general. I should have left the gizmo programming for level flight and popped the glasses off if the mask induced fogging was a distraction. I should have made the instrument scan primary rather than assuming I had more time than I actually had to program while getting to 3;000 feet.

narrative_1: Upon checking on with ATL approach; we were told to expect Runway 9R. Our initial brief was for Runway 8L because that is the typical Runway assignment when flying the CHPPR arrival. The FO (First Officer) briefed the Runway change. A subsequent Approach Controller cleared us to descend via the arrival and also that we were cleared for the ILS PRM [Precision Runway Monitor] Runway 9R approach. We had to again brief for the PRM approach because they were not advertising PRM's in the ATIS. We got a little behind the airplane and approach asked to start our descent and then handed us off to Tower. I can't recall if we were given a speed to maintain to the 5-mile fix. I checked on with ATL Tower and we were cleared to land on approximately 8-10 mile final. I recall the Approach Controller on the monitor frequency asking the aircraft behind us to slow to final approach speed. Less than a minute later; at about 1;200 feet. AGL; Tower instructed us to discontinue the approach; climb to 4;000 feet; and gave us headings. We maintained normal and stable approach at all times. We were told that the reason was because we slowed to our final approach speed at around a 6-mile final. I assumed then that we had insufficient spacing with the aircraft behind us. We were vectored for the same approach which concluded normally.We had an apparent loss of spacing on final approach which resulted in ATC cancelling our approach clearance. We were task saturated with Runway and approach changes; and with ATC instructions. We began to slow to our final approach speed sooner than ATC anticipated. We could have better anticipated the sequence of events when transitioning from the arrival to the approach.
synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported ATC re-sequenced them because they slowed to final approach speed at around a 6-mile final inbound to ATL.

narrative_1: On arrival into ZZZ; we were instructed to turn to a heading and descend from 11;000 ft. to 3;000 ft. We began a descent using speed mode set at 250 kts. Just below 4;000 ft.; we received an Obstacle Caution message. During the process of turning the descent into a climb; which removed the caution message; we were instructed to climb to 4;000 ft. I was able to identify the obstacle; an antenna; below and to the right of the aircraft. We passed the antenna above and to the left. We leveled off at 4;000 ft. From there; we were vectored to a visual approach to [Runway] XX and proceeded with a normal visual approach and landing.Descending in speed mode likely caused the aircraft to approach the level off altitude earlier than ATC anticipated thus causing the higher closure rate to the obstacle; generating the caution message. Better terrain awareness could have prompted a shallower descent rate; perhaps using vertical speed mode. Querying ATC about the level off altitude; suggesting a higher bottom altitude; could also have reduced or eliminated the occurrence of the caution message.

narrative_1: Level cruise at FL390; brief engine rumble felt and then fine.  A few minutes later; sudden onset of vibration and rollback of N1 on engine #1.  I had to go to idle on engine #1 to reduced the vibration.  We notified ATC: 'ZZZ Center; we have had an engine failure; descending to FL220 and we will get back to you with the numbers'.  At our weight and with one engine at idle; I was unable to maintain altitude; so I had to start a slow descent to our max single-engine altitude which was FL220.  The Center Controller seemed a little bit slow to recognize our situation. I neglected to squawk XXXX; which may have helped the Controller recognize what we were saying.  We repeated the call in a second transmission and then a third after he advised us to maintain altitude with opposite direction traffic at 12 o'clock.  I could see the traffic visually and it was another transport aircraft offset slightly to the south of our track.  When the Controller did recognize our situation; he advised the approaching traffic below us to turn to the south; but the traffic was already behind us and no factor at the time. The engine continued to vibrate and following the guidance of the QRH; we shut down the engine and landed at the nearest suitable airport; which was ZZZ.  It was a clear day and a single engine visual approach was completed to a landing.  The ARFF (airport rescue firefighter) crews inspected the aircraft after we stopped on an adjacent runway and advised that there was oil draining onto the pavement.  After cleared to proceed and after shutdown; we confirmed that the engine had suffered some type of internal damage and was draining oil onto the ramp.
synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported an engine failure during cruise.

Also; the Captain and I were under the belief we had until 500 feet to be stable due to the old SOPs. Furthermore; on the descent into ZZZ using the ZZZZZ3 arrival you are on with ZZZ1 Approach and do not get handed off to ZZZ Approach until 6;000 feet so you don't get a runway assignment very far out. narrative_1: While operating our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 I was the Pilot Monitoring. At the time of the event; I was eating my catering and the Pilot Flying and I both found it easier for the PF to respond to ATC and manipulate the FMS. At some point at cruise altitude; ATC cleared us to fly direct from present position to 'ZZZZZ.' The PF responded to ATC and erroneously typed 'ZZZZZ1' into the FMS scratchpad and entered the waypoint as the direct-to navigation fix after both pilots checked the resulting dashed 'proposed course line' on the PF's ND screen. After several minutes; ATC inquired if we were proceeding direct to 'ZZZZZ' as he showed us drifting right of the intended course. This alerted us to double-check our navigation and to discover that we were navigating to the wrong fix; the misspelled 'ZZZZZ1.' The PF corrected the spelling of the assigned waypoint in the FMS; proceeded direct to 'ZZZZZ' and explained our error to ATC.I can identify three things that might have prevented this event: 1) The normal procedure and best course of action would have been for the Pilot Monitoring to stop eating; respond to ATC and manipulate the FMS. I do not; however; think this was much of a contributing factor. The PF is a 'strong' and extremely competent pilot highly experienced on the aircraft. I don't think the PF's assumption of those duties was particularly taxing/burdensome to the PF as we were in cruise at a very quiet and low-threat portion of the flight. It is not unusual for a PF to respond to ATC and manipulate the radios and FMS while a PM is eating. I have always personally tried to not touch anything other than my food while eating in the aircraft and think this is an especially important practice during the current health pandemic. narrative_1: I was cleared on the RNAV departure to maintain 3;000 feet. When loading the departure an additional fix not noted on the chart was loaded in. I reloaded the departure to ensure I had the proper transition and the fix appeared again. This fix is not on the RNAV departure. I later realized that this is how the G1000 creates additional heading legs; but at the time I did not realize this and so I deleted the extraneous fix to have the flight plan reflect the proper departure.  After reaching 1;000 feet the departure states to turn left heading 295; which I had briefed. I began turning right and was adjusting the heading bug and noted it was taking a long time to reach 295 before I realized that I was turning the wrong direction. I corrected and initiated the turn back to the left heading 295. I was about 20 to 30 degrees off from the heading when ATC called and asked if I was VFR or IFR. I responded with that I was IFR and turning left to 295.There are a few contributing factors that lead to my error. First was my general lack of recency with the G1000. In the last 120 days I had amassed a total of only 6.7 hours in the aircraft. Additionally I only have a total of 24 hours in the aircraft since my check-ride last summer. This lack of familiarity; currency and comfort in the aircraft contributed to the error.  After passing 1;000 feet the G1000 was showing a magenta line to the right which is probably partially why I turned the wrong direction. An additional contributing factor was that I was operating single pilot IFR in icing conditions with little experience in the aircraft. This was a Part 91 flight and the 100 hour rule for commuter passenger operations did not apply.   While the General Operations Manual has a dual qualification policy it does not adequately address low time pilots. When a pilot is only qualified in one aircraft type they are afforded an opportunity immediately after completing their check-ride and Operational Experience to gain significant flight time and consolidate their knowledge and skills in the aircraft over the course of a few months.  In my scenario I have accumulated only 9 hours since the completion of Operational Experience. I am in full compliance with the policy and have been active in ensuring I fly the aircraft within the 90 days and make an effort to coordinate a flight when I haven't flown in over 30 days. As is evidenced by my low hours recently this does not afford a pilot new in the aircraft any significant flight time; nor the ability to consolidate their knowledge. While all aircraft are of the general purpose multi-engine variety this aircraft is the only Technically Advanced Aircraft (TAA) in the fleet. This adds a significant amount of complexity to it's operation.I would suggest that when a pilot is qualified on any aircraft we afford them the necessary time and hours to consolidate their knowledge and skills. Part 121 recognizes this issue and has the requirement for consolidation of knowledge and skills in new type aircraft. While again our aircraft are of the same type I feel with dramatic difference in this aircraft particularly; being a TAA; there should be a similar effort. Under Part 121 a pilot would be required to obtain 100 hours within 120 days of becoming qualified in the aircraft. I think we should model a policy to have similar protections. Consolidation was identified in a joint government/industry task force in 1993 to be of concern. One primary reason was 'in recent years manufacturers have introduced a greater number of new aircraft containing more equipment and systems variations within type. The complex airspace around DEN is extremely challenging; and this approach's FAF is approximately 1.4 NM from the 7;000 feet MSL Class B shelf. Descending 500 feet in less than 1.4 NM at small aircraft approach speeds does not require excessive rates of descent; but it does require a timely descent. Any delay; or crossing the FAF above the 7;500 feet MSL altitude; quickly makes it likely that an airplane may violate Class B airspace during the Final Approach Segment. In our case; the timing of the arriving Aircraft Y was coincidentally exactly the same time we were at this critical place. As a CFI-I; I am reluctant to use this approach for training ever again. One suggestion may be to cross ARRES at an altitude lower than the charted minimum of 7;500 feet MSL - if; and only if; it's a practice approach under VFR. The potential negative training this would cause would have to be weighed against the extra margin of separation from the Class B shelf. Additionally; in the future; if I use this approach for practice again; I will have the student execute a missed approach and turn away from the 7;000 feet MSL Class B shelf if the aircraft is high at ARRES; does not initiate a timely descent; or if I notice DEN traffic that could cross above us as happened on this flight.

narrative_1: Departing RJAA. I was PF (Pilot Flying). Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring). Relief FO (First Officer) was sitting in observer seat. We were within a close margin of max structural weight but within all limits. It was briefed that the best angle speed (258 kts.) and flaps up maneuver speed (254 kts.) would exceed the 250 [kts.] below 10;000 ft. restriction so we opted to keep Flaps 1 until passing 10;000 [ft.] so that we could maintain maneuverability. Once we cleaned up to Flaps 1; I opened the speed window and manually set speed to 240 kts. The overspeed margin was currently 250 kts. The underspeed margin was around 225 kts. Flaps 1 maneuver speed was about 235 kts. Upon reaching 10;000 ft.; I put 245 kts. in the speed window to initiate an acceleration that would then continue past 254 kts. for the Flaps Up speed as the flaps transitioned. The transition was going as planned until we hit some moderate wake turbulence from crossing traffic. The speed started to shoot up dramatically towards the upper limit. I applied some back pressure while keeping the AP engaged to get the nose up and arrest the speed increase. I was able to arrest most of the speed increase but it still resulted in a 1 or 2 kt. overspeed. At this time; the turbulence became more intense and both the low and high speed regimes converged. I disengaged the AP/AT (Autopilot/Autothrottle) and hand flew to best maintain airspeed as I anticipated a drop in airspeed on the other side of the wake turbulence. The airspeed started to drop but was arrested with manual input. Once the high and low speed margins stabilized and the turbulence subsided; we re-automated the aircraft and continued our departure without incident.I did not anticipate the wake of crossing traffic to be such a factor in our tight tolerances. When so close to max structural weight on TO (takeoff); the transition from Flaps 1 to Flaps Up is always on a razor thin margin. Any significant wake; turbulence or even wind shift will put you into and undesired airspeed regime. I would suggest not loading the aircraft right up to max weights and this has always been an issue for flap transition on the 767.

The first is the PASLY 4 (10-2C) arrival to BNA at GROAT intersection. The crossing is depicted to cross GROAT at or below FL 230. It is always 1000 out of 1000 times given to cross GROAT at FL 220 usually by Memphis Center and has been for at least five years. Sometimes this occurs very late. This can lead to a situation where the aircraft was on the path; is now high; and the aircraft then pitches down at the last minute to meet the unpublished altitude of 22;000 ft. This pitchdown can lead to an overspeed and a situation that still does not meet the crossing. The second instance is on the ENDEE 6 Arrival into MDW (10-2). The fix in particular is KAMBL and the published crossing is between FL 270-FL 240. The unpublished crossing that is given; very late; is to cross KAMBL at 24;000 ft. Now the aircraft is in the same situation as the PASLY 4 Arrival; only you may have a 100 plus kt. tailwind to deal with as well. Both these situations persist but are preventable by simply changing the published altitude. Finally; there are several Pilots who are rusty from not flying; due to low utilization; whose situational awareness and lack of currency make this situation even more grave. Please fix these easy to remedy issues and trap the known errors. Thank you. We did not have a deviation. I am only reporting to highlight these issues.

narrative_1: We were on the ILS 09R at PHL approximately 15 DME when the Localizer exhibited erratic deviations on both the Captain and First Officers  Primary Flight Displays. narrative_1: While on approach to ZZZ in day VMC conditions; crew was instructed to fly direct 'ZZZZZ' - the FAF for ILS XX - for a visual approach to [Runway] XX. The crew had been left high by both Center and Approach; but was able to reach the 5;000 ft. and slow prior to intercept. The PIC/PF (Pilot Flying) briefed the SIC/PM (Pilot Monitoring) on speed/energy management and airspeed 'windows' prior to the approach. After reporting runway in sight and receiving the approach clearance; the PF initiated descent to 4;500 ft. (the FAF altitude) and began to lessen the intercept angle; and PM prompted gear down and flaps 22. Aircraft still slightly overshot the localizer but was able to capture both LOC and GS which happened simultaneously. 4;500 ft. is within 1;300 ft. AGL of field elevation; and due to the short distance both vertically to the runway and laterally (just outside 4 miles); the PM/PIC anticipated an unstable approach and called a go around. The PF pressed the TOGA (Takeoff Go-Around); disconnected the autopilot; and called 'check thrust flaps nine' and the PM set flaps 9 and checked the thrust to discover the PF had not yet increased thrust to detents. Concurrently with the 'check thrust flaps 9 actions'; and 'Sink Rate' EGPWS warning occurred; and momentary hesitation by PF prompted PM/PIC to take control and initiate the immediate action in response to the 'sink rate' AURAL as required for the EGPWS escape; with a 'Pull Up' Aural warning occurring concurrently with the initiation of the EGPWS escape procedure. (At the time of initiation the EGPWS escape; PIC noted an 1;800 fpm descent rate). Upon reaching a safe altitude; the aircraft configuration was cleaned up in line as normal; and flight continued back for ILS without further incident. One error was made during EGPWS escape; which was PIC only increasing thrust to detents and not to max. Upon completion of the flight; crew debriefed on a number of key items. These included energy management and the approach profile in the AOM; go around procedure and ensuring power is set concurrently with pitch and callout when conducting a missed; and the EGPWS escape maneuver.Crews should act very early to mitigate unstable approach situations; including in a situation like this requesting a lower altitude earlier and a vector out to the IAF in lieu of the FAF; this can alleviate the chances of an unstable approach long before the issue manifests. Missed approaches should be initiated immediately upon identification of an unstable approach. In the event of a missed approach; crews should ensure the action is taken decisively including the increase of power; and both pilots should remain involved in the process. Should a GPWS warning be received; decisive; immediate action should be taken - as per the AOM - superseding normal missed approach actions due to the time critical nature of high vertical speed close to the ground. Captains especially should keep a close eye on FOs conducting operations at outstations - in this situation; having approach offer a better vector to join or taking an actual ILS clearance may have prevented the situation from manifesting at all.

As for the altitude deviation; this issue was brought to our attention by ARTCC after crossing the fix below the published crossing altitude.The cause of the electrical/ electronic failure involving the flight directors and FMC's was undetermined by maintenance and could not be reproduced. narrative_1: Arriving into ZZZ the altimeter setting was showing 0996 mb; so during our arrival brief we covered the VNAV limitation for altimeters lower than 29.70/1006 and put special emphasis on using FLCH (Flight Level Change) when transitioning. Transition level was FL070. ATC began descending us in small steps; they gave us a descend to FL070 but when we were passing FL080 they gave us a descend to 6;000 ft. then further lower to 5;000 ft.; during those step downs I missed switching the altimeter setting to the local 0996mb. Then when we leveled at 5;000 ft. ATC verified the altimeter setting stating that we were 400 ft. lower than we should have. I immediately realized my mistake; set the correct altimeter setting; took corrective action and called for the approach checklist. Since the airplane wasn't reacting as fast as I wanted; I disconnected the auto pilot; corrected the altitude and continued manual flying all the way until we landed. There is no excuse for missing an altimeter setting during transition. There were many factors/distractions that took place for this to happen and they all came pretty close together: long duty day; our bells to the flight attendants; re-route to a point not in our route; use of wing and Engine anti-ice; heavy rain during descent so continuous ignition was set; multiple small step downs from ATC; VNAV limitation; all of them occurring often simultaneously. We; as crew; came together and managed all threats that were thrown at us as best we could to bring the airplane safely to the ground.I will; from now on; better prioritize on the stuff that I delegate and ask my crew to keep an eye on me and remind me of things that could make us incur a deviation like this one. Even though we all had our hands full; I should have asked someone for some sort of reminder about the transition level.
narrative_2: At the conclusion of a long duty day and the second flight leg of the day; I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) en-route. This was my second leg as PM (6th leg as flight crew) in an international theater in nearly 3 years. Prior to descent and during the approach briefing as well as once the relief pilots entered the cockpit; we discussed the lower altimeter setting of 0996mb and the associated procedure per Company limitations from not using VNAV when transitioning from QNH (Height Above Sea Level) to QNE or QNE to QNH when below 1006mb. We felt very prepared for the arrival and descent into ZZZ. The transition altitude of 7;000 ft. was also briefed however as we proceeded; we encountered winter weather requiring extra vigilance (icing conditions and heavy precipitation). ATC descended us in multiple small increments below 10;000 ft. but the last prior to this event was a descent to 5;000 ft. With the added attention to the weather and ensuring proper use of FLCH instead of VNAV during what should have been the transition; both the pilot flying; and the pilot monitoring did not switch the altimeters at the proper time to the local setting of 0996mb. Upon level-off at 5;000 ft.; ATC came over the radio to verify local altimeter of 996mb and stating the observation of being 400 ft. low. I quickly realized my altimeter was incorrect and took corrective action and confirmed the pilot flying did so as well both with the altimeter and the flight path. One of the observer pilots also confirmed and stated the MSA for situational awareness. The pilot flying disconnected the auto pilot and continued to intercept the localizer path while returning to the cleared altitude. The aircraft was hand flown to landing with no further incident.Multiple links in the chain led up to this event and while we thought we had sufficiently briefed the several unique environments (low altimeter/Company limitation; winter weather) we also were distracted by being vectored to a point not on an arrival or the approach expected. It only goes to show that even with the best preparation and briefing that events can change and compound quickly and while attention to detail is most crucial during all phases of flight; extra vigilance is needed for approach and arrival; especially in areas that have not been flown to in recent months or years. Ultimately; the crew worked together to safely return the aircraft to the desired state and ensured a lesson learned for the future when operating in areas with differing transition altitudes.

narrative_1: On the ZZZZZ6 we were told to level at 7;000 feet for traffic. This was my 3rd trip on IOE and was practicing hand flying the departure. It was turbulent and we were in and out of IMC. Passing through 6;000 I announced that I was going to use TCS to reduce the rate of climb to about 1;000 since there was traffic above and I wanted to avoid a RA. I corrected the VS to about 1;000 ft/min. I was not quick enough to override and reduce the autothrottles to avoid increasing airspeed. The combination of hand flying in turbulent conditions in IMC and leveling at a low altitude with light loads was a recipe for distraction and error to occur. I could have eliminated some of these variables by engaging autopilot earlier or reducing autothrottles quicker. The CA and I debriefed and talked through what led to the event and how to prevent it in the future.I learned that when possible reduce extra variables that could lead to an error. I am new to flying with the company and new procedures; was hand flying in turbulent conditions and IMC; light loads with good performance; and was given a low level off. That is a lot of variables at once and the ones that I could control are the earlier use of automation to help alleviation some of the task saturation. Hand flying in turbulent conditions and maintaining altitude can be difficult and the autopilot can alleviate and sometimes do a better job to avoid deviations. Additionally I learned not to lag on overriding the autothrottles when using in FLCH mode. From this experience I feel that I can better identify and evaluate a handful of risks in a certain situation and will take prompt action to reduce these risks in a timely manner. The CA and I had a productive debrief and agreed on what variables led to the deviation and how to prevent in the future.

Upon contact with QRO Approach about 15-20 miles out; they advised of a traffic on a ten mile final; and informed us to now expect the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 Approach. We were recleared direct to QRO VOR; provided another descent; and then shortly thereafter; Approach cleared us for the approach. The First Officer went into the FMC and configured it to fly direct to QRO VOR. After the aircraft was established on course to the VOR; the First Officer selected the QRO VOR fix in the FMC and inserted the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 approach after verification with the Captain. Because of the angle the aircraft was approaching the VOR (straight in Runway 09); and relative to the approach procedure (an outbound heading 292 followed by a left procedure turn inbound); an additional procedure turn was required just to begin the approach. The procedure turn would normally be done at the VOR. Due to the FMC not having a procedure turn at the VOR to begin the approach for arrivals from the west; it immediately started auto-sequencing fixes to fly the aircraft directly to the outbound procedure turn DME 10 from the QRO VOR. The First Officer had to re-enter the VOR into Direct To and build a holding pattern into the FMC. There was a missed approach holding pattern depicted on the approach chart; therefore; the First Officer built a hold based on the holding pattern published. The First Officer informed ATC that a procedure turn was required at the VOR and also notified approach that the aircraft would enter holding as published to begin the approach. ATC advised us to descend to 11;000 feet and cleared for the approach. ATC seemed confused as to what we were doing. It appears that they were expecting the aircraft to make a hard left after crossing the VOR (almost a 180 degree turn) into unprotected airspace that contained mountainous terrain. The minimum safe altitude for that sector is 12;800 feet and if the aircraft would have flown that; there could have been a CFIT event. Once the aircraft entered the holding pattern; making a procedure turn to enter the crew selected IMM EXIT and the aircraft completed the current holding pattern; just a procedure turn; and exited the hold to fly the entire approach as planned and expected. There seems to be an issue regarding the Jeppesen Charts; and FMC database for this specific approach. The FMC did not contain any proper procedure to join the approach legally. Also the FMC sequencing the approach could have presented multiple issues including CFIT; TCAS; or lost of Situational Awareness.

narrative_1: While approaching Mt Jefferson area on course direct ELKES at 14;000 aircraft encountered a mountain wave. First indications were not unusual; a loss of altitude followed by the autopilot pitch correction to maintain and resulting indicated airspeed loss. It is not uncommon for a momentary loss of a couple hundred feet and airspeed to drop to 90 KIAS; however; at the point where it would 'normal' the situation quickly escalated into an uncontrolled altitude loss as the autopilot rapidly pitched above 15* and I noted a 90+ headwind on the G600 wind vector indicator. I immediately contacted ATC that I was unable to maintain altitude; which they issued a lower clearance (13;000) and vector away from terrain. With the autopilot turned off; I maintained about 10* nose up at 75 KIAS; flaps 10; full throttle and noted a 1200FPM altitude loss. As I approached 13;000 I informed ATC I was unable and inquired about the MVA. I was fully prepared to activate emergency power; declare; and turn back; however ATC stated that the heading I was on gave me about 9000 for an MVA. I elected to ride the wave as the uncontrolled altitude loss was trending up and was able to stabilize as I approached 12;000. While altitude was stable; I remained below the MEA and published minimum off route altitude unable to climb or increase indicated airspeed above 80KIAS for several minutes. As the aircraft exited the mountain wave to the south; I was able to recover the airspeed slowly back to normal cruise as the aircraft moved over the ridge lines.This is the second time a mountain wave event has resulted in altitude loss of more than a few hundred feet. During the 'normal' events I have always notified ATC that I was encountering a wave and only one time previous did the incident result in the necessity for a lower clearance at 13;000'. However; in this event; I would characterize the resulting altitude loss as uncontrolled at minimum control airspeed and max continuous power for the altitude. I would consider this to be an escalation of what might be a normal inconvenience; and causes me to inquire about alternate routing. In all cases of my experience; these waves seem to be encountered over the Mt Jefferson area and a southerly re-routing of to the south is the normal avoidance procedure when the waves are encountered. But why wait until one is encountered? Might it be more prudent to take a different airway further south to begin with? Might be worth exploring.

narrative_1: I was PF in the left seat and we were cleared for take off on Rwy XL.  As we were lining up on the runway; I heard the Tower clear a helicopter for an eastbound departure from the ramp; but I did not visually see the helicopter yet.  Once we were on the takeoff roll; I saw the helicopter lifting off from the ramp (ahead and to our left); but it appeared to be turning parallel to our runway to I diverted my attention back to the runway.  Right after initiating rotation; I saw the helicopter begin to cross over our runway; left to right; at approximately 200 feet AGL.  Because we were past V1 and already rotating on a short runway; I quickly determined an aborted takeoff was not an option so I continued our rotation.  During these few seconds; there were some communications between the Tower and the helicopter; but I did not comprehend them due to my focus on avoiding hitting the helicopter.  Shortly after liftoff (~100 feet AGL); I had to make an evasive maneuver to our left and reduce our climb rate for a few seconds to avoid hitting the helicopter.  Luckily; there was no terrain or obstacles to the left of our runway heading.  Once the helicopter passed off our right at what I estimate was 200-300 feet; I resumed a normal climb rate and a right turn back to our departure heading.  The Tower controller apologized and then handed us off to Departure.  Looking back on the scenario; I believe continuing the takeoff roll as we did was the right call; as we certainly would have had a runway excursion if we had attempted an abort at that point in the roll - passed V1 and already rotating.  Additionally; I am not sure how I could have anticipated the impending conflict earlier because helicopters maneuver on a dime and it was hard to tell its intending heading after liftoff.  After the event; I listened to the ATC recording on a publicly available website and it seems the controller tried to tell the helicopter pilot to remain north of the runway at all times; but that transmission was not acknowledged.

The First Officer asked me if I wanted him to go around.  There was no traffic and the runway is 2 miles long so I said to continue.  We ended up touching down at target speed well within the touchdown zone and cleared the runway.  After getting to the gate and shutting down the engines we debriefed the approach.  The First Officer said that all along he thought he was setting himself up nicely for the approach and thought it would work.  I agreed and then I took myself out of the SA loop when I started searching for the fighters and didn't pay close enough attention to our energy status.  When I finally did get back into it I wasn't forceful enough to help.  When I pointed out the engines not being at idle I assumed he would disconnect the auto thrust and put the throttles at idle.  When he didn't I should have told him too and that alone would have probably made us stable as there was still some time.  At any rate I didn't and we were clearly unstable and we both knew it.  The only correct option was to execute a go-around.  Fuel was not an issue as we ended up landing with 6;500 pounds.  I told him that I should have told him to go-around but he should have just executed a go-around without asking.  That is the procedure.  You don't need permission from the other pilot and permission not to go-around is still wrong anyway.  We agreed that the biggest factor that got us going down this path in the first place was his recency of experience and that in order to fix that he should in the immediate future at least; slow down and configure earlier then he thinks he needs to.  Going back to our departure briefing I should have taken the first leg anyway since I knew he hadn't flown in a while.  This way he could have eased back into it.
