narrative_1: Planned fuel was 6;040 and got fueled to 6;200. We took off with roughly 6;000 pounds of fuel and minimum fuel was 5;564. So we left with well above minimum required fuel according to release. We were enroute and about halfway to 2/3 of the way through as I monitored our fuel burn. I noticed based on current conditions at that time (winds aloft were greater than planned and ATC requested Mach .77 or greater while .76 is planned); that we would be about 700 pounds under planned landing fuel. So as a crew we quickly setup for long range cruise and contacted ATC that we needed to slowdown even though they insisted we maintain a high speed. So we slowed to Mach .63 for long range cruise and then ATC descended us to 27;000 feet from 31;000 feet starting down early because we were slower than surrounding traffic.Then we get instructions shortly after to change arrivals keeping us away from other traffic. Once we finally got situated with the changes; dispatch beat me to notifying them and sent us an ACARS asking about the route changes and fuel. So we told them current plan and situation and based on the information back from dispatch; we had sufficient fuel as long as we maintained LRC (Long Range Cruise speed) to ZZZ allowing us to land with just 100 pounds of fuel more than planned and dispatch had us landing at roughly 1;850 pounds. At some point ATC also queried us asking about why we would be taking off with less fuel than we need to do the flight; even though we didn't. We actually took off with more fuel than planned. ATC was actually being unprofessional about the whole thing and giving us a hard time; because we asked to slow down to conserve fuel as stated over the radios in order to avoid getting into a bad fuel situation later or having to declare minimum fuel; and then he put us on different arrival and etc. It just created more workload and pressure by his attitude and questions as if it was our fault than it needed to be and ATC did not help with that even though they're there to help us.He made us sound bad on the radio as if we didn't know what we were doing about our fuel. Then sometime later while setting up for new arrival; ZZZ does a runway change as well after we got our LDR (Landing Distance Required) and brief; so that added more workload trying to update everything and re-brief in addition to ACARS taking longer than usual to respond. During all of that; Center then instructs us to level at 19;000 feet after getting the first descend via due to VFR traffic at 17;500 feet!  After traffic passes Center then gives us descend via again with immediate handoff to Approach in the same transmission. So First Officer does the handoff while I'm assessing and starting down seeing how quick we need to descend.  I saw we needed to do 6;000 feet or more a minute in order to meet the crossing restriction. I knew that wasn't going to happen so right as I was going to tell First Officer to let ATC know we can't make the restriction because of the level off earlier due to traffic as he was checking on; Approach immediately on initial contact asked if we would make the crossing restriction and we said no.He immediately then got upset and asked if we told the previous controller who would be Center and we said no because we didn't have time as we literally just switched and got the clearance at the same time and literally a few seconds later discovered we couldn't make it work. So we explained that to Approach but he wasn't accepting that and blamed us for not making the restriction or notifying Center before talking with Approach. But we literally had no time between the clearance and handoff at the same time and during the frequency switch that's when we noticed the issue and first transmission with Approach we weren't given the time to tell him that before he asked and queried us. So Approach then gives us two small delay vectors and rejoin arrival. But Approach said we should've told them early on we couldn't make itbut again we explained the situation and that we were not given that chance to do so. So we then continued on after that with no further issues.Insufficient fuel planning on release as it never reflects the actual fuel burn since release doesn't account for delay vectors or vectors on approach. The issues with ATC and last second changes to arrival and runways were a result of not having enough fuel at normal cruise followed by slow ACARS affected our ability to fly the planned arrival causing a higher workload for us and ATC which then caused the hiccup with crossing restrictions and with crossing traffic as well.  For fuel; we slowed for LRC and got a couple shortcuts once on the banker arrival. We were able to gain most of our fuel back because of LRC and landed with 2;200 pounds. For the crossing restriction; we just explained the situation to ATC and along with Center; Approach gave us a hard time and we notified them we couldn't do it; then we carried on with no further issues after that.For fuel planning and fuel contingency; we should be doing a minimum of like 500 pounds and 750-1;000 pounds extra on IFR days. Also for holding fuel; that should be 600 pounds minimum as we realistically burn more than 400 pounds on a go-around on a VFR day. As far as ATC goes after discussing with my First Officer as the situation that unfolded after another as a result; we maybe should have declared Minimum fuel early on knowing we wouldn't have enough unless we slowed down. But because of LRC and little to no delay vectors we determined to have enough hence why we never declared. However; if we declared min fuel early on that would've maybe given ATC more understanding even as frustrating as it may be; and allow us priority to slow and not have to descend via and etc. And that maybe would've avoided the issue with crossing at ZZZZZ1 and etc. One thing led to another; so next time maybe declare min fuel and decline a descend via to stay up high longer and to reduce workload. It was a good learning experience except for lack of professionalism and help from ATC.
synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported being unable to comply with ATC speed assignments due to fuel concerns and was unable to comply with a crossing restriction due to ATC stopping their descent for VFR traffic. The Captain reported Center and Approach Controllers criticized and questioned them on the frequency over both issues.

narrative_1: After flying a practice RNAV (GPS) approach into ZZZ; I was climbing through 2;000 feet on the missed approach when I checked in with Approach. Approach provided an altimeter setting (30.12; which had changed since my last check-in of 30.11) and a few seconds later provided a heading for vectors for the ILS at ZZZ1.  I leveled off at the assigned altitude of 3;000 feet and shortly after; ATC asked me to maintain 3;000 feet.  Considering my altimeter was reading 3;020 feet; I knew this call meant something was not right.  I scanned the instruments and saw the altimeter setting was now set to 29.92. I requested the altimeter setting again and when I entered the correct setting; I was approximately 300 feet above my assigned altitude.  After landing I was able to determine the sequence of events that caused this deviation.My airplane has an Aspen Avionics Evolution 1000 PFD.  I have had this for the last X years and feel I am proficient in operating it.  It has a feature that; in my piston powered general aviation airplane; is not used.  If you press the 'baro' button and then push the right knob; the altimeter setting will change to 29.92.  Since I never climb to FL180; I have never used this feature. In this situation; when I contacted ATC; they gave me the altimeter setting; and since it was different; I pushed the 'baro' button and turned the right knob to the correct setting. When ATC then provided me a vector; I needed to move the heading bug almost 180 degrees (it had been set during the southbound approach and now I was flying northbound).  Instead of spinning the heading knob (the same right knob) 180 degrees; I pushed the knob which automatically sets the heading bug to the current heading.  What I didn't realize was that when I pushed the right knob; the 'baro' function was still active and therefore set the altimeter to 29.92.  The heading bug also aligned to the current heading; however since I was in turbulence; I assume I bumped the knob twice instead of once.  I didn't notice the change in altitude because I was in a climb.  When I reached 3;000 feet; I leveled off like normal without being aware that I was higher than I should be.Moving forward I will need to be more careful and aware of what function is active in the PFD before making changes.  However; my fear is that it may be another X or more years before something like this happens again and as time moves forward; we tend to forget these events.  I do think this is an opportunity for Aspen to make a software revision.  If this baro reset feature is meant for aircraft passing through 18;000 feet; it would be nice if this feature could be disabled for installations in aircraft that cannot reach that altitude.  Alternatively; if this feature is meant for aircraft passing through 18;000 feet and it is utilized at an altitude well below that; a flashing yellow flag (similar to what happens when approaching the selected altitude) would help to visually annotate the change that was just made. I'm not trying to remove responsibility from the pilot; but the pilot has hundreds of things to remember when flying.  Modern avionics should not be adding to the list of quirks that need to be remembered.
synopsis: PA-28 pilot reported an altitude excursion due to an incorrect operation of the Aspen Evolution 1000 PFD; which reset their altimeter to 29.92.

narrative_1: I departed ZZZ; climbed normally; received vector for a right turn to a heading of 290 and a climb to 10;000. I complied with all of the uneventfully. West of the airport was cell of precipitation that I couldn't see through. It was depicted as yellow on my weather display. The precipitation was west of the airport and oriented along the axis of about 290 to 300 west of ZZZ.I was doing the ZZZ4 departure. The tower controller advised in the initial climb that in substance that I'd be boxed around on vectors for the climb before being going to the route.A previous departed reported the ceiling at about 6;500 which was basically true. I changed frequency to ZZZ TRACON and got a heading of 290. When I entered the IMC the rain was very intense and it was turbulent. I noticed changes on the vertical speed indicator up and then later down. The temperature was near freezing; but I did not see any actual ice. While climbing in IMC; the radio frequency began to screech such that I couldn't hear anything. That ultimately occurred on both radios and both frequencies. The marker beacon lights were flashing. I received a traffic alert for traffic on my left. It was very turbulent; but I stayed at 10;000 feet as assigned. With no communications (coms); I squawked 7600.I decided to turn 90 degrees right still in IMC because that resolved the traffic; would get me out of the precipitation; was a heading basically on course; was consistent with the expectations from the departure briefing and ZZZ4; and would restore coms. The precipitation was aligned with the vector so remaining on that heading was not viable. There was traffic there. I didn't change altitude (I was at 10;000 ft. the whole time).After the right turn; I exited the side of the precipitation; I was able to hear ground responding to one of my calls (on COM2 on the bottom antenna); so I went back to the departure frequency on COM1 (on the top); re-established communications and departed.The ATC TRACON controller was upset seemed to think that I was in VMC and just turned randomly or something. I've flown through 'yellow' precipitation many times uneventfully. The lost coms procedure when you're on a vector is to either stay on the vector or turn on course. I turned on course because it solved all of the problems; but seemed to surprise ATC. I think that the confusing thing for ATC was that it was fine weather straight over the airport; which is probably what he has on his computer. But west of the airport was unexpectedly intense rain.I'm not sure that this incident could have been avoided given what everyone knew at the time; although once I squawked 7600; the turn on course shouldn't have been a surprise.

ATC brought us in on a 4 mile final from a left base which was inside the final approach fix on intercepting the final/Localizer we were slightly low but as it was a visual I told him he was a little low but I let him continue since we were stable and spooled up just below the Glideslope. anomaly: Conflict Airborne Conflict; Deviation - Speed All Types; Deviation / Discrepancy - Procedural Published Material / Policy; Inflight Event / Encounter Weather / Turbulence

narrative_1: On the arrival into the ZZZ area; ATC kept us high due to departing IFR traffic. We heard the departing traffic calling ATC on the radio after departure; but got no response. Because we were getting very close to the airport; we elected to reduce speed in order to make the impending descent easier to manage. We were monitoring both the ATC Center frequency and the CTAF frequency at ZZZ. There was a significant amount of General Aviation traffic operating in the vicinity of the ZZZ airport. As the speed was reduced below 200 knots; the First Officer; who was the PF; asked for Flaps 8 and 20. I verified that the speed was below 200 knots and selected Flaps 8 and 20. As soon as I selected Flaps 20 I realized we were still at 16;000 ft.; and said; 'We can't do that yet;' and immediately retracted the Flaps back to 0.  At this point we were only six or seven miles from the airport; still at 16;000 ft. We had identified the traffic threats on TCAS. In order to initiate our descent to the airport; we canceled IFR. After descending through 15;000 feet the First Officer again asked for Flaps 8 and 20. Because we had extended the flaps earlier above 16;000 feet; I was focused on the altitude. Due to the fact that we had slowed to below 200 knots the first time we extended the flaps; I failed to look at the airspeed indicator; thinking we were still below 200 knots. We were discussing the maneuver we would need to make to circle around and descend to the airport at the time. ATC and CTAF radio traffic was also heavy at the time. As soon as the flaps were selected the overspeed clacker started up. I looked at the airspeed indicator; saw that we were above 200 knots; and reached for the flap lever with the intent of retracting the flaps. At this point I'm unclear what EXACTLY happened next.  There was some turbulence; we were beginning our turn; and there was a lot of radio traffic.  We were also focused on the traffic displayed on the TCAS. All of this created a great deal of distraction. My hand was on the flap lever at the time; with the intent of retracting the flaps. Whether it was because of turbulence causing me to inadvertently move the lever; or me simply moving it the wrong way because of the distractions; I did; in fact; move the flap lever to 45. The overspeed clacker; interestingly enough; added to the momentary confusion. In fact; at one point I believe the First Officer said; 'What the hell is going on?' I was mortified to see the indication that the flaps were at 45; because there was no intent; plan; or call for further flap extensions. It was simply a mistake. I immediately retracted the flaps to zero. We did not receive any message associated with a flap problem; i.e. 'Flaps Fail'; etc. After everything calmed down and things were back in order; we continued the approach; which ended up resulting in a go-around because a general aviation aircraft cut us off on short final. After landing and proceeding to the gate; I wrote up the flap limitation exceedance. Maintenance arrived later; inspected the flaps; performed functional checks; found no irregularities; and returned the aircraft to service.In my opinion there were several factors contributing to the event. Distraction was probably the primary cause. We were distracted by all the radio traffic on the CTAF frequency. Sometimes it was difficult to differentiate between the CTAF traffic and the Center traffic. Also; being left so high so late on the arrival created a self-imposed sense of immediacy...'We need to get down'. Interesting to note that this urgency was never 'real'; but rather something we imposed on ourselves. Assumption was another contributing factor. Because we had originally slowed to below 200 knots; I assumed we were still at that airspeed when flaps were requested the second time. This assumption caused me to neglect the airspeed indicator before selecting the flaps because I was more concerned about the altitude.This is primarily an exercise in self-discipline and patience. The training and procedures are all in place to help prevent these types of events from occurring. It simply becomes incumbent on each pilot to be disciplined enough to not allow external factors to get in the way of simple; straight-forward procedures that can and will keep the aircraft; passengers; and crew safe.
synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reported an uneventful go-around due to an unstable approach which was caused by multiple distractions.

narrative_1: We were flying the ZZZZZ RNAV arrival into ZZZ inside of the ZZZZZ1 waypoint when ATC instructed us to descend via except cross ZZZZZ2 at 10;000 ft.; 2000 ft. higher than published. I reset the altimeter and discovered that I was actually at 16;180 ft; which likely had prompted the call from ATC.  We were just short of 200 ft high.  I descended and was at 16;000 before passing under the opposite direction traffic.  We did not receive a TCAS TA or RA.  I have no memory of resetting my altimeter to 29.92 but surmise that I must have done so as it would be very difficult to have hit the button accidentally.  While allowed to set 29.92 once assigned a climb above 18;000 ft; my normal practice is to wait until the altimeter setting flashes approaching 18;000 ft to reset it.  Normal practice meaning I don't recall ever doing it differently.  I cannot explain when I reset it to standard; except that it was after the pre-start check and prior to leveling at 16;000.  My best guess is that I did so at 10;000 for some reason; as that was the only altitude I passed that I would have considered significant; although I was on profile in a 250 knot climb both before and after 10;000 ft.  In this case; the local altimeter setting was close enough to standard that I did not exceed the 300 feet limit for a flight violation or cause a traffic conflict.  This was just luck however.  Had the altimeter been significantly different from standard; I don't believe I would have been more likely to notice the error and could have been responsible for a conflict.I'm not sure what the cause was except that I simply made an error.  Why; how; or when escapes me.  However; I did have to call in fatigued that morning as we were on a late in the day pairing but had been delayed overnight to a morning departure two time zones to the east.  When I called in fatigued unable to fall asleep early; I was given my 10 hours and a later show time; though to make the later show time I still needed to get out of bed two hours prior to when I was accustomed.  After I woke up to my alarm; I was notified that the aircraft was still in maintenance and was given an even later show time; and I took a short nap.  In the end; the error happened during a time I'd normally be awake; but I did not get my normal sleep routine.  I had legal rest and did not feel particularly fatigued; but I can't discount that fatigue very well could have contributed to such an unusual error.  I utilized the Fatigue Risk Management Plan (FRMP) to the extent I felt necessary and neither Crew Scheduling nor the company pressured me in any way to fly fatigued.  Perhaps I should have insisted on an even later show time.  My feeling of responsibility to our customers who had already been delayed over 12 hours was a factor in making a show time that was earlier than normal for me; considering time zones; but again; I didn't feel overly tired at the time. Obviously; having made this error for the first time; I'll be more cognizant of when I hit the button to bring the altimeter to standard going forward.  As far as the possible fatigueaspect; our promise to our customers to transport them to their destination at the time we say can sometimes conflicts with our promise to transport them as safely as possible.  I have availed myself of the risk management plan several times in the last year and have never received any negative feedback or pressure to fly fatigued.  There are times when I feel the probability of losing pay has pressured other pilots to fly with less rest than they needed; but in this case pay was not a factor as I was the only pilot available to fly this leg to an outstation serviced only once per day.  So; I was going to be paid for the leg no matter when I flew it.  Therefore; I can't recommend any changes to the risk management plan.  I simply need to do a better job of anticipating and assessing my own fatigue level.

Aircraft X was taxied to Runway 1R on the SSTIK4; which requires a red 'R' if requested/required by the pilot.  It is unknown at this point if that was the case.  My only assumption is that the Ground CPC-IT taxied the aircraft incorrectly to Runway 1R and the OJTI did not notice.  As their flow time came up; Local CPC-IT taxied Aircraft Y across Runway 1R at M and LUAW Runway 1L.  Aircraft X was given Runway 1R LUAW.  The CPC-it then; unbeknownst to the OJTI; launched Aircraft X on the SSTIK4; and shortly thereafter launched Aircraft Y also on the SSTIK4.  The only reason I became aware is when I heard the CPC-IT issuing visual separation and the Local Assist coordinating the same with NorCal.  When I looked up at the display; the aircraft were approximately 2 miles in trail with Aircraft Y lower and following to SSTIK.  Of note; with OJT occurring on both Local and Ground simultaneously; and Local Assist open; but apparently not engaged dynamically; the FLM could not possibly monitor both positions and all that the Local Assist was doing.  Subsequent discussion by the Local Control OJTI dictated that they were sorry; as they missed it and 'Use of RNAV To... will save you every time.' The numbers of neigh-sayers are reducing thankfully and we will eventually have the majority compliance.The traffic has picked up over 700 operations a day a few days of the week and is expected to get busier by the month this summer.  Use RNAV To... and; when working as OJTI; pay attention to what the CPC-IT is doing.

narrative_1: On the departure; the First Officer (FO) had requested Heading Mode (HDG); Flight Level Change (FLCH) during the climb out as we were given a heading.  It was bumpy and he was trying to comply with the SID instructions to speed up to 250 KIAS while hand flying in bumpy air.  As we approached the 5;000 foot altitude restriction; he started to slow his climb for the level off; but didn't pull back on the thrust levers. The autothrottles were on; but we were not quite close enough to the altitude for the flight director to switch to 'ASEL' on the FMA and begin capturing. In a climb; the auto throttles remain at full thrust in green FLCH until ASEL is annunciated; and since the FO was hand flying and beginning the level off before the Altitude Select (ASEL) annunciation; the speed began to pick up.  As pilot monitoring; I noticed the airspeed at 255 KIAS with an increasing trend and I called out 'airspeed' to alert him to the airspeed.  He seemed confused and did not make any corrections. I then called for him to 'pitch up' which he did slightly; but he mentioned the level off altitude that was approaching.  I said to 'pull the thrust back' and he seemed confused again and replied that the auto throttles should do that.  I then pulled the thrust levers back myself to slow the aircraft down as the speed was starting to go past 260 KIAS.  ATC gave us a 'climb and maintain 7000' and a direct to one of the fixes.  The FO pitched up for the climb and I was able to let go of the thrust levers as the speed was again under control.  As we were climbing; ATC instructed us to climb to 16;000 and the FO called for 'Autopilot On' prior to the next level off so there were no further issues.  I reminded him that there is no speed protection in the level off for the FLCH mode if he is hand flying it and levels off early.   ATC didn't seem to notice the increased airspeed;  and the flight continued without further incident.The FO said that he finished IOE and for the next month was unable to get any flying from crew scheduling.  He had less than 30 hours on the aircraft.   The following month; he had to be in Country to check on family due to the COVID pandemic.  He said that he had flown earlier that day and seemed to be comfortable in the plane.  It became clear that he was rusty on the details concerning the FLCH mode.  After I spoke with him about what happened; he said he understood and he did not make the same mistake on his flight the following day. Any time a pilot has less than 100 hours (consolidation) on an aircraft; and doesn't fly for more than 30 days; they should be given a trip with an IOE instructor both to give them recency of experience and to refresh any forgotten material.
narrative_2: During take off climbing to the assigned altitude of 5;000 in flight level change plane accelerated to 250K; during last 1;000 ft I shallowed the pitch as climb was getting a bit bumpy due to builds up around [the] area and I was trying to avoid flying through a cloud straight ahead. Captain advised me of speed increasing and passing 250 and I assumed the auto-throttle would have compensated for that as it was engaged. Leveling off to 5;000 speed past 260 and the Captain reached out the thrust lever decreasing power avoiding further deviation. Soon after cleared to 7;000 climb and flight continued with no further deviation. After IOE I was put on reserve and didn't fly for about a month; I then was able to pick up a line and fly just one sequence as a tragic event forced me to drop the rest of the month and travel overseas; as a result in 2 months I only flew 19 hours and that was my first day flying after a long stop. As newly typed on a new airplane I didn't immediately recalled the different ways the autothrottle responds; however soon after the event my Captain explained [to] me what happened and refreshed my memory on it. After IOE it would be good to assign some extra flight to help consolidate; maybe assigning more frequent flights and not letting more than 2 weeks without flying would avoid skills deterioration until the first 100 hours are reached.

narrative_1: I was in the traffic pattern doing touch and go landings with a student at ZZZ (one of five aircraft in the pattern).  We were approaching mid-field right downwind for Runway XX; and tower advised that we were following another aircraft on base; which we advised we had in-sight (which was number two; making us number 3.) As we approached our base leg; tower told us the base turn was our discretion; and we began turning base.  As soon as we did so; the traffic we were following (Aircraft Y) called tower and advised that they needed to do a 360 for spacing (it appeared they had turned their base leg too soon; and were too close to the traffic they were following.  Tower approved and notified them that once they completed their 360 to watch out for us; and that they would be now following us (making us now #2 for the runway; and them #3).My student turned final and we were on an approximately 1.5 nm final; descending through 700-800 feet; when my student stated; 'I think they're turning right at us!'Simultaneously Aircraft Y had apparently just completed their 360 turn and Tower inquired if they had us in sight and were to follow us; they stated they were looking for traffic.I looked up to suddenly see the other aircraft heading directly across our final approach path; and almost on a head-on course; coming at us approximately from 45 degrees off of our left nose.  As I looked; I also simultaneously received an ADS-B traffic alert from Foreflight on my iPad; indicated the other traffic; heading directly at us and at the same altitude.I immediately stated 'my controls'; took over control of the aircraft; and quickly began a descending turn to the right to create distance from the other traffic; I looked up again and saw the other aircraft also start a sharp bank to their right; while simultaneously telling the tower that they now had us in-sight.  I remained in control of the aircraft and executed an (otherwise) uneventful landing.Tower did not acknowledge the event.  It seemed that the controller was very task saturated with the five aircraft in the pattern.  It seemed they were also distracted by a King Air 350 that was handed over to tower from ZZZ Approach and setup for a right downwind for Runway XX. Initially tower had told them to enter left downwind; but they were adamant that they wanted right downwind; which I believe both added to the confusion; as well as tied up the tower frequency unnecessarily with their continued back and forth communications. It did not help that the King Air had requested and was then doing a 360 turn for spacing of their own; right on the upwind leg of Runway XX when there were multiple other aircraft in the traffic pattern.It should be noted that while we were on short final; the Aircraft Y involved in this incident had once again turned base too soon; and I noticed that they were less than 0.5nm behind us.  They were so close that they in fact were ordered to go-around by the Tower because we had just touched down and were still rolling out when they crossed the runway threshold behind us.I believe contributing to the incident were: The pilot of Aircraft Y failing to maintain situational awareness resulting in inadequate spacing thus requesting multiple 360 turns; their failure to adequately scan for traffic and maintain a proper rectangular course in the traffic pattern causing them to cross our final approach course at a 45 degree angle; tower controller being task saturated with multiple aircraft in the traffic pattern; and the King Air traffic adding to the confusion by adamantly requesting to enter the right downwind (which conflicted with the other aircraft already in the traffic pattern for Runway XX; which is right traffic.)

narrative_1: I was Pilot Flying. I triggered a stick shaker/pusher at the Final Approach Fix. I recovered per SOP.[There was] a northbound squall line west of the field. ATC forgot to turn [us] on the ILS; so we went through the localizer course. This led to reactionary vectors and the aircraft doing S turns until we passed the final approach fix. At this point we were flaps 30 with the power reduced. I called for the go-around; but when I pressed the autopilot disconnect button; I became fixated on the lack of a missed approach course. (I didn't press the TO-GA button.) While troubleshooting; the airspeed continued to decrease leading to a simultaneous stick shaker and pusher. I lowered the nose and recovered per the training; paying special attention to the radar altimeter. I briefly oversped flaps 8 on recovery.Stall recovery training works. I was able to accomplish the recovery quickly without having to think about it. However; it shouldn't have gotten that far. It was my first go-around since OE. I was task saturated and in the moment couldn't remember where the TO-GA button was. We were able to handle weather; ATC error; runway changes and an instrument approach at the same time. However; because our go around was triggered at a relatively untrained aircraft state/position; I missed a critical aspect of the maneuver. I don't believe this is a common problem; but incorporating go-arounds during recurrent in various positions may be beneficial.

narrative_1: While in cruise at FL400; I noticed cabin altitude display illuminate Amber on upper EICAS showing cabin altitude of 8300 feet and rising at 300-400 ft/min.  Aircraft was dispatched with one pack deferred; two operating. I brought up the ECS schematic to verify Packs 2 and 3 were both supplying pressure and in High Flow. They appeared to be operating normally; but I then noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault; cabin altitude was already 9;000 ft. and still climbing. At this point I requested a descent from ATC to FL 360.  They gave us a vector for descent.  A minute later; with Cabin altitude of 9300 ft.; I informed ATC we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend.  We were given FL390 and then a few minutes later; FL360.  Pressurization stabilized at 8;500 ft.; but began to climb again at 100-200 ft/min. We requested and were given FL 320.  I notified Operations Control via ACARS (SATCOM inop); that we had a Pack 2 issue and that we had descended as cabin altitude had been increasing. They were given our fuel and told I would keep them advised. We were at FL 280; where cabin altitude at stabilized; but showing slight increase. I recommended to divert to ZZZ along our route of flight; but they informed me they wanted the airplane in ZZZ1.  I informed ATC that we needed to change our destination for 'maintenance' from ZZZ2 to ZZZ1.  We were given proceed direct ZZZ1; about 350 miles away; where we landed uneventfully.Cruise flight when cabin altitude appeared amber on Upper EICAS.Strictly a maintenance issue with the aircraft. We had Pack 1 deferred and any issue with the remaining Packs was going to cause pressurization issues.To assess the situation; attempt to bring pressurization under control; and descend as necessary to reduce cabin altitude.  QRH was utilized to validate what pressurization reading we should have at the various altitudes.Aircraft was dispatched to pick up freight in ZZZ2; and then proceed with a Pack deferred.
narrative_2: Pushback; taxi; takeoff and climb were completely normal. Weather on departure were calm winds and decent VFR in the terminal area. The weather became more marginal upon leveling at cruise. On this leg I myself was the First Officer and Flying Pilot. The Captain was the Pilot Not flying. We also had a Relief Pilot on board and loadmaster.  The event began somewhat early in cruise at FL400 when the Captain noticed a cabin altitude display Amber on the Upper EICAS display. He then immediately selected the ECS page and we both were made aware of a 8;300 foot cabin and rising at 300-400 fpm. The aircraft was dispatched with Pack #1 deferred; therefore packs 2 and 3 operating normally. After diagnosing the situation via the ECS page; both packs 2 and 3 appeared to be supplying pressure and in High Flow as designed when one pack is selected off.  However on the Lower EICAS we both noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault. Cabin altitude was still climbing and at this point showing 9;000 feet and still climbing. At this point we agreed to suggest a decent to FL360 and were given a vector for decent. About a minute later with Cabin Altitude of 9;300 feet the Captain informed ATC that we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend now; we first were given a decent to FL390 and shortly after to FL360. At FL360 we observed the cabin initially stabilizing at 8;500 feet; but shortly afterwards began again climbing at a lower rate than previously of 100-200 FPM.  We again agreed to request a lower altitude of FL320 and ATC cleared us to FL320. The Captain then notified Operations Control of the situation via ACARS (SATCOM Inop) that we had a PACK 2 issue and we were descending with a cabin altitude still slowly increasing. The Captain requested further decent to FL280 and ATC complied. At FL280 we experienced a cabin altitude almost stable at around 8;000 feet but still trying to climb at a slow interment 100 FPM. The Captain notified the rest of the crew including the Relief Pilot and load master. The Relief Pilot was taking his rest but immediately returned to the cockpit to help in CRM and dealing with the situation. I suggested the Relief Pilot pull up the cabin altitude chart showing what the cabin altitude should be for our current altitude so we would know how far off from normal we were.  All 3 crew members talked about possible diversion airports and relayed our ideas to Operations Control. After communication between Operations Control and us it was decided by Operations Control to divert to ZZZ2 to address and fix the situation. The Captain immediately requested to divert to ZZZ2 and informed ATC as to why; and I put us on a course to ZZZ2 via ATC instructions. At this point we were about 350 miles north of ZZZ2 with plenty of fuel and sufficient weather for landing. We landed at ZZZ2 uneventfully and maintenance was made aware of the present maintenance issues.While in cruise flight the cabin altitude appeared amber on the Upper EICAS.Pack 2 was failing for unknown reasons. Pack 1 was already deferred on departure so any remaining pack issues was going to cause a pressurization issue.Crew did their job in noticing the system fault and working the problem. We were dispatched with Pack 1 deferred so any further pack or pressurization faults would cause a pressurization issue.Dispatching an aircraft with a pack deferred which would and did cause a pressurization issue when any further pressurization problems would happen. In this case pack 2 also failing to perform up to specification; therefore; causing an increasing cabin altitude at a higher level cruising altitude.

narrative_1: On final approach to Runway 13 into MDT; we were cleared to intercept the visual final approach course. I mistook the Capital City airport (CXY) Runway 12 for MDTs Runway 13. We were asked if we had MDT in sight; thinking we did; and cleared for a visual approach; I made a descent for CXY Runway 12; still not realizing it was not MDT Runway 13. narrative_2: We were approaching Harrisburg Int'l from the west when we were instructed to intercept the final course for a visual approach to RWY 13. It was hazy with visibility low enough that the only airport in sight was Capital City (CXY).  Its RWY 12 is oriented similarly to RW 13 at MDT; so when we were asked if we had the airport in sight; we said we did.  The airport was closer by a few miles than our FMS was indicating so we configured for landing and steepened the approach. MDT Tower then asked if we could be approaching Capital City as we were lower than we should've been. At that point; MDT was also visible. Interestingly; the proximity of these two airports is compounded by the fact that the airport on the south side of the river (CXY) is actually north of MDT; which is on the north side of the river due to bends in the river.We could've avoided the error if we'd been more familiar with the area and/or declined the visual approach.

narrative_1: I have departed ZZZ airport to the south to practice landings in ZZZ1. On the way back to ZZZ I have contacted ZZZ Tower around 7NM to 8 NM south of the field; the Tower has replied standby so I have tuned to easterly heading so I will not enter the airspace; a few minutes after that the Tower has instructed me to join mid left downwind for Runway XX and to report when established on the downwind; after I have established on the downwind I have notified the Tower. To the best of my knowledge and memory the Tower has replied the following instruction: 'you are number 3 for Runway XX continue'; I have given the Tower read back and then I looked forward to visually scan for the traffic in front of me; I remember clearly that I saw 2 aircraft in the final for Runway XX; the first one was an airplane in the short final and the second one was a helicopter that was also in the final behind him. I remember that I have pointed the 2 aircraft to my students and explained to them that these are the aircraft that are in front of us and we will follow them as we are number 3 in the sequence. After the helicopter was abeam to my position; I continued to fly on the downwind for an extra 30 seconds to 1 minute so I will allow some extra spacing between myself and the helicopter as I'm flying with students on their first ever fly day. As I was told I'm number 3 in sequence and I visually saw the 2 aircraft that are in front of me I have continued the traffic pattern and turn left to the base leg; and then when I was in the appropriate position I have turned final. Between 30 seconds to 1 minute after I was established on the final for XX the Tower has instructed me to 'immediately turn heading 090 and break the approach'; I have immediately took controls from my student and turned to the heading 090 while giving a read back to the Tower. As I have established on the heading 090 I saw that there was a jet aircraft on the final approach behind me; approximately 1;200 feet horizontally and 300 feet vertically in my evaluation. after that I have continued to comply with the Tower instructions and followed a different traffic that was on the downwind to join the final for Runway XX again for a full stop. Before landing when I was on short final I have verified with the Tower that I had clearance to land.I have strong belief in self critic and self evaluation and after this event has occurred I have come up with the following safety measures that can help prevent this situation from reoccurring:1. When you have been instructed to follow traffic while on the downwind; you should always verify with Tower that you can start your turn towards the base leg.2. When you are told that you are number 3 in sequence and you see the 2 aircraft in front of you; that absolutely does not mean that you should stop looking for other traffic in the area; you still need scan for traffic very frequently.3. When flying on the base leg; even in a controlled airport; you should always try to look for more traffic coming on the final; both behind you and in front of you; and make sure that there is no traffic that can jeopardize the approach before actually making the turn to final.4. Do not think that just because you are flying in a controlled airspace under ATC supervision; you are protected. Always actively scan for traffic and verify ATC instructions.I believe that if I had used these safety measures that I have mentioned above this event could have been prevented. What else could I have done...I allowed myself to get distracted. I should have continually monitored the lateral path to insure the AC was doing what we thought it was going to do. The aircraft began a descent per the VPATH glide slope. I ran through the items again to verify that the approach was proceeding correctly. I verified again that the FMA's showed an engaged green LNAV and engaged green VPATH. The approach was proceeding as expected. At the CEPEE waypoint; the aircraft should have begun a right turn towards the AAGEE as part of the track towards the final approach point and final approach course. narrative_1: We were taking off from ELP on Runway 22 and had an initial clearance for the TDOWN3 RNAV Departure.  Tower cleared us for takeoff with revised clearance to turn left to 200 and climb to 17;000 [feet].  I was the flying pilot manually flying.  As we were accelerating and getting the aircraft to a clean configuration we were issued a frequency change to Departure.  Upon checking in we were immediately given further instructions which included a right turn after reaching 6;200 feet to 060.  Both of us misunderstood the turn right part of the clearance.  The FO (First Officer) read back 'passing 6;200 heading 060' and had no response from the controller.  We climbed through 6;200 and turned left. We were about half way through the left turn when the controller saw the mistake and told us it was a right turn; but then told us to continue the left turn.  He later asked us to call them for possible pilot certificate action. There are several causal factors [due to direction of turn by flight crew].  First; having a clearance for an RNAV departure that has a left turn from Runway 22 sets you up to expect a left turn out for protected airspace even after receiving a last minute change to the departure plan using radar vectors.  Because the radar vectors are given last minute the old departure stays in the FMC showing the original route on our map displaying that left turn; so even though we were not following the route displayed it probably influenced our thought pattern.  There is no published departures turning out to the right from Runway 22 due to mountainous terrain if you are departing east.  Secondly; we also had prebriefed the engine failure procedures that have you turn out to the left for the same reason.  Third; from a 200 heading to turn right to 060 is counter intuitive because it is more than 180 degree turn. All of these factors I think caused expectation bias to turn left and not hear the right turn instruction.  Fourth; the controllers failure to emphasize the right turn part when it is more than 180 from current heading and his not ensuring the read back was correct. Controllers need to emphasize the direction of turn especially if it's more than 180 degrees and ensure they get a correct read back.  On the phone the controller said this was normal to avoid traffic from Mexico.  If this is a common procedure to use radar vectors to turn us out an opposite direction of our assigned clearance then there needs to be some notes somewhere in our charts so we can prepare for that ahead of time.  This non published procedure could cause conflicts with terrain in the event of an engine failure.
narrative_2: The missed approach and takeoff engine failure profiles for Runway 22 tell you to turn left.  The TDOWN 3 SID; we were assigned; tells you to turn left off of Runway 22.  The reason all of the departures turn left on Runway 22 at El Paso is because there is high terrain if you turn right.  On takeoff; we were told to climb to 17;000 feet and turn left to heading 200.  When we contacted Departure; the controller quickly blurted out a long; involved clearance.  I responded; 'Passing 6.2; turn to 060.'  He did not respond back to my radio call.  On a heading of 200; the heading of 060 is to the left.  As we entered the left turn to 060; the controller informed us that he had told us to turn right to 060; he also told us to expedite our left turn and continue to a heading of 010.  When we rolled out on the heading; he told us to call a phone number because of a potential violation.  I read the phone number back to him and asked him to verify.  He did not respond because he was working two frequencies; and was talking to another aircraft on the other frequency. When we called the phone number for El Paso Departure Control; they told us that left turns off Runway 22 often conflict with traffic at a Mexican airport.  So; they often vector you to the right.  The Captain and I have both been in and out of El Paso numerous times; and have never gotten a right turn off Runway 22.  None of our guidance for El Paso says to expect a right hand turn.  Expectation bias caused us to hear 'turn to 060' instead of 'turn right to 060.'  Also; the Departure Controller was working two frequencies and did not catch that we said 'turn to 060.'  Here is what he blurted at us at 1;000 feet AGL while we were retracting the flaps; '[company name]; radar contact; turn right to 060 and climb to 17;000.'  He also had a thick; Hispanic accent.  If the keyword was 'right'; it didn't help that he placed it in the middle of a sentence with no emphasis or follow up. If left departures off Runway 22 conflict with Mexican air traffic; perhaps they need an updated departure procedure.  The ATKNN 5 Departure off Runway 22 turns right; but it continues west bound.  There are no departure procedures for Runway 22 that turn right initially; and then continue to the east.  Also; none of our guidance tells us to expect a right turn off of Runway 22.

It seemed to me that Dispatch was adamant about diverting to ZZZ3. We also discussed other airport near ZZZ1 (off field) that could be potential alternates. After the check in with Approach they asked us our intentions which we replied stand by and began rough fuel calculations to ZZZ2. The Captain quickly determined that fuel to ZZZ2 was inadequate due to a 15-20 minute flight and approximately 2200lbs of fuel on board. (Increased fuel burn at lower altitude; storms in the area; and potential unknown issues on arrival at ZZZ2). We then asked ATC about aircraft success in to ZZZ1 which they replied that some aircraft were making it in and some were not. We then requested Runway XYR because it was the closer runway and informed ATC of our minimum fuel situation. The Captain notified the Flight Attendant; we ran the appropriate checklist (ATIS; build it; bug; brief it) and continued vectors to Runway XYR. There were two aircraft in front of us which one was able to land and another missed (aircraft in front of us) due to wind shear. After recalculating fuel requirements the Captain determined that a missed would put us in an emergency fuel situation therefore we [advised ATC]. I believe that upon intercepting the localizer we were somewhere around 1700-1800lbs. During the approach the gains and losses of altitude did not seem significant but it appeared to be difficult to maintain the localizer although I did not see anything greater than one dot. There was also added pressure to continue the approach due to the fuel situation. During the approach tower asked the aircraft that made it in where they broke out and they replied 'right at mins'. At around 800 feet I called out that I could see the ground which was not visible as we got to 500 ft. At 300 feet I called approach lights in sight 12 o'clock and continued to call out the approach lights. The aircraft began to drift right and I called the runway environment insight at 11 o'clock. Throughout this period it was apparent that the Captain was having difficulty seeing the runway. When he finally looked up and determined that he did not have adequate references; and the aircraft was not in a safe position to land; he called the missed. Immediately on the missed it was apparent the at least 90 percent of the airfield was VFR. We could see all of Runway XZ/XA; including approach paths; so we made a decision request XZ and due a VFR pattern into XZ. Tower provided we could use whatever runway we needed so we continued with XZ; entered the left crosswind; base; and landed. During the miss we did not climb to the missed approach altitude; left the gear down; and kept the flaps at nine because of the immediate landing after the missed to Runway XYR. We updated the FMS with Runway XZ and extended a line for reference because there are no approaches in our pubs for XZ. We did not rerun the performance information again because the field length was 10;500 [feet] which was longer than Runway XYR and it was an immediate landing. We also received fuel EICAS alerts during the missed and a fuel critical prior to landing XZ. All approaches were conducted with flaps 22. Emergency vehicles were on scene which we did not require. Upon taxiing into the gate the field went in to a ground stop due to lightning. In all the entire flight segment from door closed to door open was 3.4 hours. I would say that this flight provided the crew with several threats. To name a few; my PFD was inop so only the CPT could fly; windshear; GPWS; and TCAS were inop; pop-up weather wasoccurring throughout the flight route; fuel considerations; ACARS not accurate due to new AOM changes; delays prior to departure; delays in route; other aircraft encountering wind shear; and potentially an inexperienced dispatcher. There was also a significant pressure to land the second approach. I felt that we handled the situation very well as a crew and discussed and analyzed any and all potential alternatives but were cornered due to the fuel situation. I do wish I had analyzed the winds better throughout the duration and been more aware of the weather at the field during the Runway XYL wind shear event. With most of the airfield being VFR it was absolutely possible to successfully complete approaches to the XB runways and XZ/XA [runways]. The only area impacted by the weather was the XY runways approach segments. Therefore; if winds were within landing limits we could have immediately requested an alternate runway from ATC.
narrative_2: While conducting the setup check in ZZZ; the GPWS Inop; Windshear Inop; Terr Inop; and Terr Fail messages appeared on the EICAS. Maintenance was called and the affected system was deferred per MEL. The aircraft also had an MEL for the First Officer MFD; and an NEF item in the cockpit. ACARS would not produce accurate weight and performance numbers; and Dispatch informed us that this was a known issue. We elected to perform a manual weight and balance with the Form X. The TAF for ZZZ1 was forecasting VFR and radar looked fairly benign. The First Officer obtained the D-ATIS for ZZZ1 which showed Winds Calm; visibility 10SM; Few at 5000; Scattered at 8000; with no other weather (information M). Due to this; extra fuel for weather was not considered by us or Dispatch. While in our initial descent the First Officer and myself noticed the weather in ZZZ1 was deteriorating and sent an ACARS to Dispatch asking if we should get an alternate. Dispatch replied that no alternate was needed; and we assumed that they had more up to date information than available to us in the air. Our radar was depicting areas of extreme return (red and purple) blanketing the approach and airport with other aircraft saying it was a smooth ride; but heavy precipitation. While outside of the final approach fix on the ILS Runway XYL; other aircraft were heard going missed due to windshear. ATC informed us that some aircraft were landing and some were going around. We elected to continue the approach as we were not experiencing any abnormal flight conditions. Inside of the final approach fix; I was unable to maintain positive aircraft control on the approach path due to airspeed; altitude; and course fluctuations. I made the determination to execute a windshear escape/go around. The Flight Attendant was notified of our situation. We contacted Dispatch to request a diversion and suggested ZZZ2. Dispatch replied that ZZZ3 was a better option; but ATC informed us that ZZZ3 was having similar weather to ZZZ1. I used the FMS to determine a rough fuel burn to ZZZ2 as 1400 lbs not including any deviations or approaches. We were also low on fuel; approximately 2;200 lbs after the missed approach. We discussed and agreed that we did not want to end up in ZZZ3 with such low fuel and similar weather issues. We decided to attempt a second approach at ZZZ1 after ATC stated that some aircraft were landing successfully. It was apparent that we would be below divert and possibly final divert on the second approach so we declared Minimum Fuel. We requested ILS Runway XYR due to perceived improved conditions and the closer approach for that runway. During the approach; the Flight Attendant called and said that a passenger was in the bathroom and asked if we could delay the landing. I advised her that due to our fuel situation; it would not be possible. She was able to get the passenger back to his seat before final approach. While on the approach; we overheard the aircraft in front of us go around for windshear. Our fuel level was low and a go around would put us in a fuel critical situation. We [advised ATC] and continued the approach. We experienced difficulty in maintaining the approach course and I used my PIC authority to continue the approach since a missed approach would leave us with inadequate fuel for much option. The First Officer called approach lights in sight; and we continued to 100 feet above the field. The First Officer called Runway in sight; and when I looked up; I did not see a runway and was disoriented due to the extreme precipitation and reduced visibility and immediately executed a go around. We were now showing a very low fuel level; and it was unlikely we would have enough fuel to get to another airport or reattempt an approach. I used PIC emergency authority to request a circle to land Runway XZ. We were able to maintain visual contact with Runway XZ during the maneuver. We had no time to get any type of performance numbers; and reasoned that since itwas longer than Runway XYR we could land. The landing was conducted without incident. As we engaged E/TO Reserve on the windshear escape; I entered this in the logbook and contacted maintenance. See attachments for reference if needed.Many threats existed in this incident including: pop up weather; weight restrictions; the need for paper performance calculations; an inoperative MFD; an inoperative Windshear system; and lack of an alternate. The weather and TAF looked ok during the planning portion of the flight; it was not until enroute; that everything deteriorated. I believe we acted in the best manner possible given the stressful situation and lack of backup options (fuel and/or alternate). It was a unique scenario that required a unique response. I believe we made safe decisions based on the current parameters. In hindsight; I would have been more assertive about requesting an alternate enroute. I do not believe we could have forecasted such bad weather; which is why we did not ask to remove passengers to add fuel in ZZZ. As we could not find a suitable alternate; we had little choice once we were low on fuel than to attempt to land on any runway. A third go around would have likely had us considering an off field landing.

narrative_1: During the terminal phase of a single pilot IMC maintenance ferry flight to MRN (Foothills Regional) I requested the RNAV (GPS) Runway 21 Approach into MRN. ATC approved the request and cleared me to the CIKIS IAF. Scanning the preloaded route of flight in my G1000 PFD; I inadvertently selected the CICAC FAF as the desired steer point and turned in that direction. ATC observed the aircraft tracking to the wrong fix and directed a heading change in the direction of the IAF. At that instant; I detected the switch error and made the appropriate correct selection. The approach continued and the flight terminated without further incident. There can be no excuse for my having failed to confirm the exact GPS steer point selected; but in the interest of preventing a future incident such as this; I might question why two of the fixes on this approach would be labeled with identifiers so similar in spelling and pronunciation that this error could almost have been predicted; especially in the high workload environment of single pilot IMC during the terminal phase of the flight. I suspect that I'm not the first pilot to bite on this one; and the controller was probably spring-loaded to detect and correct my error. Can't TERPS label these fixes with less ambiguous identifiers?

narrative_1: I set up for a visual approach with an ILS back-up to Runway 13L at DAL.  We were in good shape from a speed and altitude standpoint at NNATE.  I was hand flying.  I was distracted by the localizer guidance which showed me well right of course when I was actually slightly left.  I mentioned that to the Pilot Monitoring.  While troubleshooting the lateral guidance; I got behind the jet for getting flaps 15 and gear down and we ended up high.  As I regained my crosscheck; I subconsciously followed vertical guidance; which now was taking me erroneously higher. I called for flaps 30; and realized we were now 800 feet. The Pilot Monitoring called out the PAPIs (Precision Approach Indicators); which showed all white; but the glideslope guidance was taking me higher.  I called for a go-around.  My go-around was sloppy; but the Pilot Monitoring brought his A game; so it was manageable. On the second approach; a visual approach backed up by the ILS 13L; both lateral and vertical guidance were erroneous.  I had to fight the tendency to cue on the vertical guidance; which again was taking me high. The Pilot Monitoring turned off both flight directors. On short final; we got an audio glideslope alert. The glideslope raw data showed me way low. The PAPIs were three white and one red.  We should have also turned away from the ILS on the NAV tuning panel. On both approaches; an Aircraft Y was parked right at the hold short line in front of the glideslope antenna.  I suspect we will see more aircraft stopped at the hold short line with the runway closure at DAL; and so we will see more ILS interference.  I have seen similar ILS behavior at other airports with an aircraft stopped at the hold short line.  We did not write up the aircraft.  An ILS test was completed and passed prior to the flight. NOTAM (or other reminder) that the 13L ILS may be unreliable with aircraft in the ILS critical area. More training on go-arounds.
synopsis: An Air Carrier pilot reported they received erroneous glideslope and lateral guidance from the ILS while an aircraft was holding in the ILS critical area. The reporter stated this will become a recurring issue due to a runway closure at the airport.

narrative_1: On the ORCKA 5 Departure; after passing the 160 SMO radial and DOCKR below 3;000 feet. We were given heading of 030 and climb to 12;000 feet as prescribed by the SID (expect vectors). As we were climbing and turning he gave us direct 'KLIPR at or above 10;000; climb to 15;000.' I could not find KLIPR on the legs pages. I checked several downline pages; went back to page 1/9 and then checked the route page to verify the ORCKA 5. It was loaded but still no KLIPR. I told the controller it isn't apparently on our route. He spelled it out. I was moving too slow. He gave us 030 heading and told us to let us know when we are heading there. I though we were heading in the right direction but the intersection is now behind us. As I was jamming the box; perhaps KLIPR got eaten or dropped out as we passed it. It's location is right by DOCKR.  I can't figure out why it wasn't there initially as we turned. We were going through 10;000 feet easily so he then gave us direct KEGGS and to go to next frequency. The next controller gave us direct NNAVY.  Altitudes were no issue; if anything our climb rate was quicker than my cumbersome effort towards KLIPR. What could we have done better. I had expectation bias from the old Loop departure. If I remember after DOCKR you loop back to LAX at or above 10;000 feet. With this departure giving an initial vector and our climb rate much better than my 737 experience.  I was looking for KLIPR to be farther down the road than between LAX and DOCKR. I still don't know why I didn't see it because I was looking at the' top of the flight plan' legs page. I was just too slow for the expectation of the controller so he vectored us on down the line. Although I haven't been to LAX in two years I am comfortable there and fell behind unexpectedly during this event. Errors were automation Management; FMC / CDU and similarly spelled waypoints.
narrative_2: The following narrative describes events that occurred over a very short period of time; perhaps only a few minutes in total. It is my sincere intention not to cast blame; but to offer an explanation for what happened from my biased point of view as the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X. Our flight began normally from LAX; with the exception that we were pushing back about 45 minutes late due our aircraft's late arrival into Gate 77. Preflight duties were performed fairly routine; but under some time pressure to complete everything thoroughly but as quickly as we could in an attempt to make up some of our delay. This time pressure was self-induced; as no other employee was pushing us for an on time arrival in ZZZ. Red flag #1. During the pre-departure cockpit preparations; we received notice that the passenger boarding was complete; followed shortly by ramp informing us that they were ready for the parking brake release and pushback. At this point I gave a cursory PF brief from the briefing card we all carry - too cursory. Red flag #2. Taxi and takeoff were normal from Runway 25R on the ORCKA5 Departure. I was manually flying; enjoying only my second flight as PF in over a month. We switched from Tower frequency over to SOCAL Departure; and shortly after checking in we received instructions to continue climb I believe to 5;000 feet and turn left to a heading of 030 degrees. Quickly after that we were given further climb to 12;000 and direct to KLIPR.  At this point things went wrong; rapidly. The Captain; as PM (Pilot Monitoring); couldn't find the KLIPR intersection on the legs page; and informed ATC that it did not appear to be on our departure. SOCAL spelled out the intersection phonetically; and then I think confirmed that we were on the ORCKA5. Things were happening fast. While hand-flying; in the turning climb; I tried to locate (unsuccessfully) KLIPR on the 10-3 page displayed on the iPad. Red flag #3.At this point; I should have turned on the autopilot to assist with the FMC and MCP inputs; as I could detect the stress and frustration in the Captain's voice in being unable to find KLIPR on the legs page; or on the departure plan view. Red flag #4. In my divided attention between flying the aircraft and searching for KLIPR on my iPad; I failed to find it as well. I was looking too far down the flight segment to see that the this waypoint is located right off the departure end of the 25s at LAX. This was the key moment; I think; and the last opportunity to correct the error. All I needed to do was put on the AP (autopilot); join the Captain and assist with the repair. But I did not; at least not immediately. The Captain inserted KLIPR on the legs page; got my confirmation; and executed the entry. When I had looked at the route modification; I thought it was correct. The waypoint showed in the correct direction (I thought) but much further down line than it should have; off the scale of my selected range on the navigation display. Red flag #5. Passing around 10;000 feet I engaged the autopilot at the Captain's urging to finally get back in the cockpit as a crew and together correct the problem. I engaged LNAV; but we were not turning fast enough for ATC and the controller gave us a new heading of 010.  I'd like to add at this point that our controller was patient; helpful and professional throughout our fiasco. The only way he could have helped us more is if he teleported into the cockpit and handed us our crew meals. Somewhere in the fray I had suggested that we reload the departure and that would bring KLIPR up; and now the legs page had a discontinuity and we had lost the LAS transition. Also we were given further climb; and now the KEGGS intersection to get us back on the departure. It was at this point I saw we had not been heading to KLIPR at all; but to 'CLIPR'! How did I miss that?! I had set up that problem by not giving proper confirmation of the legs page entry; having not used proper procedures (see Red flag #5). Further climb; and now direct to NNAVY were issued; but we first had to reload the lost LAS transition. After that was competently accomplished; our 'helmet fire' was apparently extinguished; and we were switched to the next Departure Controller. He gave us direct Las Vegas; and kindly spelled 'LAS' in the clearance for the lost crew.What followed was probably a good 2 hours of discussion and self-examination of what went wrong and why. I believe that two primary factors set us up for these errors. The first was my too-brief departure review. This was the first time the Captain had been on this departure; and only my second. Although we both verified the FMC route and legs page; and had confirmed the proper altitudes; we were not familiar with all the new (to us) waypoints; such as KLIPR. A more thorough review on the ground was paramount; and I failed to do it. The second was my desire to manually fly the aircraft during what rapidly became a complex departure. At the first sign of things getting too busy; it became mandatory for me to engage the autopilot; and thereby engage my brain in helping eliminate the threat. I failed in that regard. Adding mistakes such as 'CLIPR' vs. 'KLIPR'; was due to my attention being more in the HUD than on performing proper FMC verification procedures. That was entirely on me. I still have no explanation for why KLIPR was not on the legs page. I had displayed on my CDU the Takeoff Ref page; and did not give due diligence to the ND or the legs page on the Captain's side. What I saw was '_ _ IPR'; and a magenta line in the direction I wanted to go. Not good enough!  Additionally; in my attempt to find KLIPR on the Jepps I zoomed in and slid the page right-to-left; taking the desired waypoint right out of sight. Using the autopilot undoubtedly would have enabled me to do this search more thoroughly. We had only seconds; it seemed; to prevent this entire undesired event.

narrative_1: This was in a B737-8 MAX which is not selectable on the menu.  Inbound to ZZZ; deviating west of the arrival due to a severe TS over ZZZZZ and also another TS touching ZZZZZ1 along with multiple significant CB radar returns just west of our direct line to ZZZZZ1.  We checked in with ZZZ Center and descended to or level at FL340. We were made aware that our deviation west of the arrival was causing the Controller difficulty in de-conflicting our descent due to departing traffic which was below us and to my understanding west of us.  Very busy controller with no time to discuss options.  I was approaching the west edge (absolutely as close as possible) of the last significant CB when the Controller told us in an excited tone to turn right 15 degrees and descent to FL280 (or maybe 240; I don't recall now).  The CB was about 4 mile ahead and 2 miles across in both directions and 15 degrees right would put us straight through the middle of it.  I started an immediate right and tried to ask my First Officer to tell the Controller we had to have farther right; but he saw me turning and read back the 15 degree instruction.  The Controller was immediately on to two or three other calls.  I asked my First Officer to tell the Controller the heading that we needed to fly and about then the Controller noticed that we had turned a bit extra and shouted at us because apparently another aircraft was departing in the corridor between the last CB and the big TS.  I immediately corrected back and flew through the middle of the CB I was trying to avoid which was where the Controller wanted us in the first place.  I also paused my descent very briefly to verify with the Controller that we were going to be safe still and we agreed on a heading of north as we passed directly through the cell.  Fortunately; despite passing though the small cell with a solid yellow return; there was no significant turbulence and no injuries.  I don't believe we caused loss of separation and my intention was to coordinate and return to the desired heading as soon as possible. The frequency was too busy; departures probably should have been pushed farther west; I was trying to comply with the Controller's guidance as best I could while not creating a dangerous turbulence situation for my flight attendants and passengers.  The B737-8 MAX radar might be overly sensitive.  Had the Controller asked 30 seconds sooner we would have had time to coordinate; or a minute later we could have taken any heading.  In retrospect; we should have said we were unable to turn for another 6 miles; but given the urgency in the Controller's voice; I thought I was doing the right thing.Whenever an airplane is cleared to deviate for weather and is operating around thunderstorms and significant CBs; it seems like the Controller should always ask if you can accept a turn; not just assign a heading into the direction of the things we are avoiding.  Also; if there is any way to make these frequencies less congested; that would help also.  And finally; the other company's aircraft was apparently flying outbound and closer to our assigned arrival than we were comfortable with flying inbound.  Maybe ZZZ Center should develop and publish alternate Departure and Arrivals that could be assigned for weather avoidance as widespread thunderstorms are so common in this area.

narrative_1: At GS intercept; 2000; on the ILS XX and as I was setting the missed approach altitude; 2;500; the outer ALT ring was in 1;000s increments. He successfully landed; we cleared the runway; and taxied to the gate.Slow is smooth and smooth is fast. In my haste to correct a simple mistake; I made a blunder. No fault go-around policy is great! There's no way of knowing if we'd have seen the slat lock if the first approach was flown to a landing. I had approximately XX hours on type.

narrative_1: Arriving in TUS we had briefed the RNAV RNP Y Rwy 11 approach.  Our clearance was for the ZONNA 1 arrival which took us from SSAND to OTUKE.  Just outside SSAND we were cleared to fly the lateral course for the RNAV Y.  We cleaned up the box and turned on to the course.  The next fix was LUYEG; our clearance was to cross at 11;000 feet cleared for the RNAV Y approach.  We slowed to 240; went flaps 1; did the LAVS procedure.  The FMA went to PATH and looked normal.  We read the Approach checklist.  I checked the FMAs again; it indicated SPD not PATH.  There was no VNAV scale to indicate high or low on the path.  I selected V/S and slowed the rate of descent.  Before I could enter the next stepdown altitude in the MCP; ATC called with a low altitude alert.  There was no EGPWS warning.  I disconnected the A/P and initiated a climb.   We were in VFR conditions.  We reengaged the A/P and selected 9;500 feet for a crossing altitude at HODPU.  We did the LAVS procedure outside of HODPU.  The FMA went to PATH and looked normal until it crossed the fix and then it went to speed.  After that we used the A/P to fly the lateral course put each crossing altitude in the MCP.  On final I disconnected the automation [and] flew a visual approach.  First Officer did an excellent job monitoring; calling out deviations; and analyzing the problem.
